INTRODUCTION

Teaching one unified Special Speaking classroom

This Teacher's Book is designed so that you can walk into your Special Speaking classroom ready to run an engaging, clear, and productive lesson without having to invent missing explanations, answer keys, follow-up prompts, or timing plans.

In a real Special Speaking class, learners sit in the same room with a wide range of fluency and confidence — from solid intermediate speakers who still hesitate over tense choices or word order to more advanced speakers who are ready to refine their register, nuance, and rhetorical control. Rather than splitting the room into separate tracks or handing out different worksheets, the Student Book teaches the whole class through one shared learning journey. Every student participates in the same opening conversation, learns from the same clear explanation and side-by-side contrasts, and engages in the same pair and real-talk tasks.

Differentiation happens naturally through the richness of each student's spoken response and through how you guide them in the room. Each lesson guide in this book gives you concrete ways to support developing speakers (so they can participate accurately and confidently in the shared task) and ways to stretch stronger speakers (through deeper follow-up questions, added nuance, and the precision patterns in Part 6) without ever labeling or segregating learners.

Across all sixteen guides you will find: clear lesson objectives and observable success criteria; board and preparation notes; a practical 60-minute timing plan (plus a 45-minute adaptation); step-by-step guidance for all eight lesson parts; quick concept-check questions; complete Practice A and B answer keys with explanatory notes and acceptable alternatives; model pair exchanges and Real Talk responses; mixed-classroom support and extension strategies; targeted remedies for common misunderstandings; and fluency-protecting feedback routines.

Three habits of effective delivery

Before and during class

• Let students speak first in Part 1 before you explain any grammar on the board — those first two minutes create curiosity for the rule.

• Keep everyone on the same task: use sentence starters or board prompts when a pair needs support, and ask 'Why?', 'Under what conditions?', or 'How could you say that more precisely?' when a pair finishes early.

• Protect spoken fluency during Parts 5 and 7: listen and note recurring slips quietly, then run a brisk three-minute board repair after everyone has finished speaking.

Assessment architecture

• Diagnostic Test (25 written items + matched baseline speaking sample) — before Lesson 1.

• Review Test 1 after Lesson 4 (Lessons 1–4); Review Test 2 after Lesson 8 (Lessons 1–8); Review Test 3 after Lesson 12 (Lessons 1–12). Each review test assesses only taught material.

• Final Assessment after Lesson 16: 30 written items sampling all lessons, plus the matched two-minute speaking task and four-criterion rubric.

• Five student reference appendices: Grammar Formula Book, Common Errors Guide, Essential Sentence Patterns, Can-Do Tracker, and the Complete Answer Key (Appendix 5).

TEACHING PRINCIPLES

Eight habits that make grammar stick in conversation

1. Situation and meaning before terminology.

Begin every lesson with a concrete human situation and let learners talk in Part 1 before introducing any rule. When a grammatical term is needed, explain what it means in everyday English.

2. Keep explanation brisk; give the hour to speaking.

Parts 1–3 should take roughly 15 minutes in total. The remaining 45 minutes belong to active practice, pair conversation, precision building, and the unscripted Real Talk Challenge.

3. Teach contrasts side by side in the same context.

Students rarely understand a structure in isolation. Show how changing 'I lived' to 'I have lived' or 'mustn't' to 'can't' changes the real-world message in the listener's mind.

4. One classroom, open-ended depth.

Never split the room into separate tracks. Give the whole class the same communicative task; help hesitant speakers land a clear, accurate core answer while prompting confident speakers to elaborate with reasons, stories, concessions, and the precision patterns in Part 6.

5. Models are inspiration, not scripts to memorize.

Have learners attempt the speaking task first before uncovering the printed Model Response. Then ask them to notice one useful phrase or connection in the model and try a second round.

6. Correct without interrupting communication.

During pair work and Real Talk, listen with the printed criteria and jot down two or three anonymous sentences on a notepad. Put them on the board after the timer ends so the whole class can repair them together.

7. Honour legitimate grammatical alternatives.

English often allows more than one natural form depending on the speaker's focus (for instance, present perfect simple vs continuous, or 'may / might / could' for possibility). Credit every accurate option noted in the key.

8. Close every lesson with active recall.

In the final five minutes, ask students to close their books and produce the target patterns from memory. Retrieval without looking at the page is what builds real-time fluency.

Adapting to different class schedules

• 45-minute session: follow the 'Shorter-session adaptation' box in each lesson guide — keep the 15-minute explanation and 10-minute practice intact, run a focused 12-minute Pair Speaking + precision round, a 5-minute Real Talk sprint, and a 3-minute recall check.

• 90-minute session: run the full 60-minute plan, then have students switch partners and repeat the Real Talk Challenge on a second topic, incorporating feedback from the first round.

Fluency-protecting feedback routine

While students are speaking — listen and note

• Circulate quietly with the lesson's success criteria; never interrupt a speaker mid-thought to fix a grammar slip.

• Write down two strong sentences you hear and two recurring errors on your notepad (without student names).

• If a pair stalls, join briefly as a curious listener and ask one natural follow-up question to restart the flow.

After the speaking round — repair in three minutes

• Start by praising one specific communicative success and one strong sentence from the room.

• Write the two anonymous error sentences on the board and invite pairs to spot and repair the pattern in 30 seconds.

• Have the whole class say the repaired sentences aloud once so the natural rhythm lands in everyone's ear.

LESSON 1 · TENSES FOR REAL COMMUNICATION — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: talk about habits, experiences and changes accurately

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Choose accurate verb forms for habits, temporary current situations, finished past events, experiences connected to now, and future plans or arrangements in spoken English.

• Explain in plain English why a finished time expression ('yesterday', 'last week', 'in 2020') requires the past simple rather than the present perfect.

• Deliver an unscripted one-minute account of how their English or another practical skill has improved over time, combining past simple, present perfect, and present simple/continuous.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ at least 4 of 5 Practice A items are completed accurately before the answer key is discussed

✓ corrections in Practice B are justified with a clear time or state-verb reason rather than a guess

✓ in the Real Talk Challenge, time expressions match the speaker's chosen tense consistently

Before class begins:

• Draw four simple columns on the board: NOW & AROUND NOW (present simple / continuous) · CLOSED PAST (past simple) · CONNECTED TO NOW (present perfect) · NEXT (future choices).

• No handouts are needed; learners jot down only three keywords during Real Talk planning.

• Optional: encourage learners to use a phone voice-memo app to record their one-minute Real Talk response so they can hear their own tense choices afterwards.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two opening sentence pairs aloud ('I live with my cousin' vs 'I'm living with my cousin until my flat is ready'; 'I lost my keys yesterday' vs 'I've lost my keys — can you let me in?'). Ask them to explain what changes in real life between each pair without using grammar terms.

• Give pairs two minutes to answer the two personal hook questions ('What does a normal weekday look like for you, and what temporary project are you working on this month?' and 'What is one important thing that has changed in your daily life over the past year?').

• Take two brief responses from the room, write the time phrases learners used under the board columns, and point out that today's lesson makes those tense choices automatic.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Walk through the three core rule groups in order: Rule 1 (Present tenses: baseline habits/facts vs temporary spotlight), Rule 2 (Past simple vs present perfect: closed time vs open bridge to now), and Rule 3 (Future choices: decided plan vs instant decision vs fixed calendar arrangement).

• Have the class read one natural example per rule box aloud so the rhythm of contractions ('I'm working', 'I've sent', 'I'll carry') lands in their ear.

• Write 'I saw him yesterday' and 'I've spoken to her recently' on the board to show why finished time stamps lock the door on the present perfect, while 'recently' allows either tense depending on the speaker's focus.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'Last year I…' — which tense follows, and why can't we use 'have + participle'? (Past simple, because 'last year' is a finished time period.)

• 'Nadia has worked here since 2022' — does Nadia still work here today? (Yes — 'since 2022' bridges past to present.)

• Contrast 'I'll help you carry that' with 'We're meeting the director at ten tomorrow' — which one was arranged before this conversation?

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Ask learners to cover the right-hand column of the 'Present perfect vs past simple' table in Part 3 and predict with a partner what the listener hears in each pair before uncovering it.

• Read the 'State verbs vs action verbs' section together. Contrast 'I think this course is practical' (opinion = state) with 'I'm thinking about applying for a scholarship' (active mental process happening now).

• Run a 30-second check: call out three time expressions ('last night', 'since 2022', 'these days') and have the class name the matching tense.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (5 items) individually, then 1 minute to compare answers in pairs and read each completed sentence aloud.

• Run Practice B (4 items) in pairs: insist that for items 1 and 2, learners state both the corrected sentence and the one-sentence reason why the original failed.

• Confirm answers with the whole class and clarify any item where learners hesitated.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. saw · 2. has worked / has been working · 3. are meeting · 4. is snowing · 5. believes

Practice B: 1. I finished my assignment last night. ('last night' is a finished time) · 2. She knows three foreign languages. ('know' is a state verb) · 3. have you known · 4. I'm going to study medicine next year.

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'saw' — 'last week' names a finished past time; 'have seen' is never grammatical with a closed time marker.

• A2 accepts both 'has worked' and 'has been working' — 'since 2022' connects the past to now, and both simple and continuous aspects are natural with 'work' and 'live'.

• A3 'are meeting / 're meeting' — a fixed personal arrangement with a specific time word ('tomorrow morning at ten') naturally takes the present continuous.

• B3 'have you known' — 'know' is a state verb (so not 'have you been knowing'), and 'How long' asks about a duration continuing up to now.

• B4 'I'm going to study medicine next year' — 'be going to' expresses a prior personal intention naturally in conversation.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange ('How it sounds in conversation') aloud with a volunteer so everyone hears how a natural follow-up question grows out of the partner's answer.

• Put learners in pairs to interview each other using the four questions in Part 5, requiring at least one unscripted follow-up question after every answer.

• Close the round by asking two learners to report one interesting change or current project they learned about their partner.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: What are you doing these days that wasn't part of your routine six months ago? B: I'm walking to class every morning instead of taking the bus, and I listen to English podcasts on the way. A: That's a great habit. How long have you been doing that? B: Since March — I've listened to about thirty episodes so far, and my listening has improved a lot.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Guide the whole class through the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): each learner says three true sentences about their own week — one permanent habit, one temporary project this month, and one experience they have had this year.

• Move together to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): model the present perfect continuous ('I've been revising all morning, so my eyes are tired'), a combined past-setback + present-growth sentence, and the milestone frame 'It's the first time I've ever…'.

• Have pairs build one sentence of their own using either the present perfect continuous or the past-plus-present-perfect contrast and share the strongest examples with the room.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners exactly 30 seconds to jot down three keywords only (one past turning point, one change up to now, and one current habit or focus) — no full written sentences.

• Have partners take turns speaking for one full minute while the listener tracks the four items in the Partner listening checklist. Keep the printed Model response covered during round one.

• Have learners uncover the Model response, notice how it links 'Last year I joined…', 'Since then, my confidence has grown…', and 'These days I listen…', and then deliver a tighter 45-second second attempt to a new partner.

Student Book model response:

I've been studying English seriously for about two years. Last year I joined a weekly speaking club, and that was the moment things really changed for me — I learned to respond in English right away instead of translating every word in my head. Since then, my confidence has grown a lot, and I've spoken in front of visitors twice at work. These days I listen to a short news podcast every morning while I walk, and I'm focusing on making my pronunciation clearer.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Use the four Partner listening checklist items as live criteria while circulating; do not interrupt speakers mid-minute.

• Credit any natural response that names a specific past turning point (past simple), explains progress up to now (present perfect), and describes current habits or projects (present simple/continuous).

• Note two recurring tense/time mismatches anonymously on your notepad for a three-minute whole-class board repair after the speaking round.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Have learners close their books and answer the two active-recall prompts in Part 8 orally with their partner.

• Ask everyone to tick the four 'Can I do this in real speech?' checkboxes honestly; point anyone with an unticked box to the matching rule in Part 2 and Formula Book Card 1.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the four-column board timeline visible throughout Pair Speaking and Real Talk so hesitant speakers can glance at the time cues before choosing a verb form.

• Offer simple spoken starters on the board: 'Last year I…' · 'Since then, I have…' · 'These days, I'm…'

• If a learner struggles with finished vs open time in Practice B1, practice swapping 'last night' and 'so far this week' on the same sentence aloud before starting Part 5.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Invite confident speakers to weave past simple, present perfect, and present perfect continuous into their Part 5 follow-up answers (e.g., explaining both how a change started and how long they have been working on it).

• Ask early finishers in Part 6 to explain the subtle difference between 'I've spoken to her recently' and 'I spoke to her recently' using a real example from their week.

• During the second Real Talk round, challenge confident speakers to include one 'It's the first time I've…' or 'This is the most… I've ever…' milestone frame naturally.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'I have finished my assignment last night.' → 'I finished my assignment last night.' — Fix: ask 'Is last night finished?' Whenever a closed time stamp appears, use the past simple.

• 'She is knowing three foreign languages.' → 'She knows three foreign languages.' — Fix: remind learners that mental states ('know', 'believe', 'understand') stay in the simple form.

• 'We will meet the director tomorrow at ten' for an existing appointment → 'We're meeting the director tomorrow at ten.' — Fix: reserve 'will' for spontaneous offers/predictions and use present continuous for calendar arrangements.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run questions 2 and 4 in Pair Speaking with one follow-up each.

• Do the first block of Part 6 orally in class and assign the three nuance sentences in the second block as short spoken/written homework.

• Run one 60-second Real Talk round followed by a brisk two-minute model comparison and exit check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Use the two closed-book recall prompts in Part 8 as a quick oral exit ticket.

• Remind learners that both 'has worked' and 'has been working' are accepted in Appendix 5 for open durations with 'since' and 'for'.

• Open Lesson 2 next session by asking three learners to share one sentence about yesterday (past simple) and one about their week so far (present perfect).

• Feedback focus: While pairs speak, jot down two strong tense contrasts you hear and two anonymous sentences where a finished time word clashed with 'have/has'. Put both on the board after Part 7 and let pairs repair the slips together in 60 seconds.

LESSON 2 · TELLING STORIES AND DESCRIBING EXPERIENCES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: tell a story with background, sequence and clear focus

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Tell a clear personal story that separates the background scene (past continuous), the main events (past simple), and an earlier past action (past perfect).

• Use time and sequence markers ('while', 'when', 'by the time', 'at first', 'suddenly', 'in the end') to guide the listener smoothly through a narrative.

• Deliver an unscripted two-minute story about a memorable trip, problem, or surprise and retell it more concisely in a second round.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ each spoken story includes at least one background clause (past continuous) and one earlier-past clause (past perfect)

✓ the partner can retell the key events in the exact order they happened without confusion

✓ at least three natural sequence markers are used to connect the stages of the story

Before class begins:

• Write the four-part story arc across the board: SCENE (was/were -ing) → MAIN EVENTS (past simple) → EARLIER CAUSE (had + participle) → ENDING / TAKEAWAY.

• Write the contrast pair 'When the guests arrived, we cooked dinner' vs 'When the guests arrived, we had cooked dinner' on the board for Part 1.

• Have a visible timer ready for the 10-second silent planning window in Part 7.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two dinner sentences in Part 1 aloud and decide in which house the guests ate immediately and in which house they had to wait.

• Give each learner 60 seconds to tell their partner a brief story about a small problem from the past month (a late bus, a forgotten item, or a sudden change of plan) while the listener notices how the background scene was set.

• Highlight how the three past tenses act like camera depth — background, foreground action, and flashback — so the listener never gets lost.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (the three past levels) using the board arc: past continuous for the scene in progress, past simple for the chain of events, and past perfect for what had already happened before the main moment.

• Teach Rule 2 ('when', 'while', and 'by the time'): have the class chorally practise 'While I was walking down the street, the rain started' and 'By the time we reached the stop, the bus had already left.'

• Teach Rule 3 (story shape and sequence markers), emphasising that a memorable story closes with why the moment mattered.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'While I was walking' vs 'When I walked' — which connector naturally introduces a longer background action in progress? ('While' + past continuous.)

• Write 'By the time we arrived, the film had started' on the board — which happened first, our arrival or the start of the film? (The start of the film.)

• Can we use 'would' for a past state like 'We would live in a small house'? (No — use 'used to live' for past states, and 'would' only for repeated past actions.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the three-column table in Part 3 ('Same situation, three different time signals') so learners see how changing one verb form changes the timeline of the train and the meeting.

• Read the four-stage story arc table together ('Stage 1: Set the scene' to 'Stage 4: Give the outcome and takeaway') as a blueprint for Parts 5 and 7.

• Ask: 'Which tense answers What was already in progress?' (past continuous) and 'Which tense answers What had already happened earlier?' (past perfect).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, followed by a 1-minute pair check focusing on how 'by the time' (A2) and 'by 2019' (A5) trigger the past perfect.

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners combine and repair items B1–B5 aloud and then build their two-sentence rain story for B6.

• Check answers whole-class and have two volunteers read their B6 mini-stories aloud.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. was studying · 2. had already eaten · 3. called / took · 4. was walking / saw · 5. had finished · 6. were playing / was resting

Practice B: 1. While I was reading the contract, the office printer jammed. · 2. By the time we reached the station, the train had left. · 3. When I arrived at the hall, the speaker had already left. · 4. answers vary · 5. while · 6. It was raining hard, and because I had forgotten my umbrella at work, I got soaked. (answers vary)

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A5 'had finished' — 'By 2019' establishes a past cut-off point, so an action completed before that point takes the past perfect.

• A6 'were playing / was resting' — two simultaneous background actions in the past naturally take the past continuous in both clauses.

• B3 'When I arrived at the hall, the speaker had already left' — repairs the timeline so the departure clearly precedes the arrival.

• B5 'while' — 'was having a shower' is a longer background action interrupted by the doorbell.

• B6 is open-ended — credit any natural two-sentence story that combines 'was/were raining' (scene), 'had forgotten' (earlier past reason), and 'got soaked' (main event).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how a listener asks a curious mid-story question ('Did you miss your stop?') that prompts a past perfect explanation.

• Give each partner two minutes to tell a true story from one of the four prompts in Part 5 while the listener prepares two follow-up questions and a three-sentence retell.

• After both partners have spoken, ask two listeners to share their three-sentence retell with the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: Last winter I was travelling home on the evening train when the power suddenly went out. B: Did you get stuck for long? A: Almost an hour — by the time the backup generator started, my phone battery had already died because I hadn't charged it at work. B: How did you let your family know? A: A kind passenger lent me his phone, which turned a stressful evening into a great conversation.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Work through the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic') together: have pairs take one simple event ('I missed the bus') and expand it aloud into a 30-second story using 'while', 'when', and 'by the time'.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): introduce 'would + base verb' for nostalgic past routines, the past perfect continuous ('had been waiting for an hour when…') for duration before a past event, and a present perfect takeaway ending ('It taught me a lesson I've never forgotten').

• Have each learner craft one closing takeaway sentence for the story they told in Part 5.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 10 seconds of silent mental planning (no writing) to picture the opening scene, the main turning point, and the earlier past cause of their story.

• Round 1: Learners tell their two-minute story to Partner A while Partner A checks the four items in the Partner listening checklist.

• Have learners read the printed Model response, notice its sequence markers and closing reflection, and then switch to Partner B to tell the same story a second time — smoother, clearer, and more concise.

Student Book model response:

It was a Friday afternoon in May. I was walking home from the bookshop when I suddenly realised I had left my phone on the counter — I had only been walking for ten minutes, so I turned back at once. At first I checked my coat pockets twice; then I hurried back down the street. By the time I reached the shop, the owner had already answered a call from my cousin: he had won two tickets to the championship final and needed my answer straight away. I called him back from the shop counter, and we went to the stadium that evening. I've checked my pockets before leaving every shop ever since.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen against the four Partner listening checklist criteria: opening scene (past continuous), clear sequence markers, earlier-past flashback (past perfect), and a meaningful closing line.

• Accept any authentic personal story; if a speaker forgets to include a past perfect clause, ask one natural question at the end ('What had already happened before you got there?') to elicit it live.

• Compare the first and second tellings in Part 7 — praise smoother pacing and clearer time signalling in the second round.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral retrieval tasks in Part 8 (explaining the difference between 'When I arrived, they left' and 'When I arrived, they had left', and telling a three-sentence mini-story with 'while' and 'by the time').

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 2 if any box remains unticked.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Leave the four-stage story arc on the board during Parts 5 and 7 so developing speakers can point to each stage as they move through their story.

• Provide five sequence starters on the board: 'It was a… afternoon and I was…' · 'At first…' · 'Suddenly…' · 'By the time…' · 'In the end…'

• If a learner strings everything together with 'and then… and then…', have them pause and insert one 'while' scene and one 'because I had…' reason before the Real Talk round.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to open their story with a nostalgic routine ('Whenever we visited my grandparents, we would…') before shifting into the specific day's events.

• Challenge stronger speakers to include one past perfect continuous clause ('We had been driving for three hours when…') to build tension before the turning point.

• Ask listeners in confident pairs to challenge one detail with a follow-up question that requires a past perfect answer ('Why hadn't you checked the schedule earlier?').

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'When I arrived at the hall, the speaker already left.' → '…the speaker had already left.' — Fix: draw two points on a timeline and label the earlier past point 'had + past participle'.

• 'While I was walking home, I was seeing an old friend.' → '…I saw an old friend.' — Fix: the shorter interrupting event takes the past simple.

• Flat endings ('…and then I went home.') — Fix: ask 'What did that experience teach you?' to prompt a one-sentence present perfect takeaway.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; limit the Part 5 pair stories to 90 seconds per partner.

• Practise the 30-second expansion in Part 6 in class and assign the 'would' / 'had been -ing' extensions as homework.

• Run one telling in Part 7 and use the second telling as the warm-up at the start of Lesson 3.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one sentence combining 'while' and 'when' or 'by the time' and 'had' before leaving.

• Save the four-stage story arc — learners will reuse it in Lesson 13 (reporting conversations) and Lesson 16 (final synthesis).

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 2 in Appendix 1 for quick review.

• Feedback focus: In Part 5, let the listener's three-sentence retell serve as immediate communicative feedback: if the listener got the order of events right, the storyteller's tenses worked. Then put two anonymous timeline slips on the board for a quick whole-class repair.

LESSON 3 · QUESTIONS, AUXILIARY VERBS, AND FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: ask clear questions and keep a conversation alive

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Form accurate direct questions (with auxiliary inversion) and polite indirect questions (with embedded statement word order) in real-time conversation.

• Distinguish subject questions ('Who called you?') from object questions ('Who did you call?') without inserting unnecessary 'do/does/did'.

• Keep a two-minute conversation flowing naturally using short reactions, content-based follow-up questions, and echo or tag questions.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ indirect questions in Practice B and Pair Speaking keep the verb after the subject ('Could you tell me where the station is?')

✓ learners ask at least three follow-up questions that react to the specific content of their partner's answer rather than changing the subject

✓ subject questions are formed without 'do/did' when 'Who' or 'What' is the subject

Before class begins:

• Write the two contrasting word-order frames on the board: DIRECT = Question word + Auxiliary + Subject + Verb ('Where does the bus stop?') vs INDIRECT = Polite opener + Question word + Subject + Verb ('Could you tell me where the bus stops?').

• Write four quick reaction + follow-up stems on the corner of the board: 'Really? How did that happen?' · 'That sounds intense — what did you do next?' · 'How about you?'

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two exchanges in Part 1 aloud — Exchange 1 (an interrogation that kills conversation) vs Exchange 2 (a natural conversation with a reaction and follow-up). Ask: 'Why does Exchange 2 feel so much more human?'

• Run the one-minute hook challenge: Partner A makes one simple statement ('I tried to cook a new dish last night') and Partner B must keep the conversation going for 60 seconds using only short reactions and follow-up questions.

• Point out that great conversationalists rely on three tools: clean question word order, polite indirect openers, and genuine follow-up questions.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Direct questions): highlight the auxiliary-before-subject pattern ('Where do you work?', 'Did she call you?'), then contrast subject questions ('Who called you?') with object questions ('Who did you call?') on the board.

• Teach Rule 2 (Indirect questions): show how a polite opener ('Could you tell me…', 'Do you know…', 'I was wondering if…') already does the job of asking, so the rest of the sentence returns to normal statement order.

• Teach Rule 3 (Follow-up questions): have the class read the three-step rhythm aloud — React briefly → Ask about a specific detail → Invite the partner back.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'Do you know where is the bank?' — why does that sound wrong to an English listener, and how do we fix it? ('…where the bank is' — no inversion after 'Do you know'.)

• 'Who phoned you?' vs 'Who did you phone?' — in which question are you the person making the call? ('Who did you phone?')

• After 'Did she…', do we say 'called' or 'call'? ('call' — 'did' already carries the past tense.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Use the Direct vs Indirect table in Part 3 as a choral call-and-response: you read the blunt direct question on the left, and the class answers with the polite indirect question on the right.

• Compare the Subject vs Object table ('Who broke the window?' vs 'What did the wind break?') and ask learners why 'do/did' disappears when the question word is the doer.

• Do a 30-second board check: write 'Do you know what time is it?' and let the class repair it aloud.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, paying special attention to A3 (embedded word order) and the A5/A6 subject-vs-object pair.

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners say their polite indirect rewrites (B1–B2), repair B3, and practise two natural follow-up questions for B4 aloud.

• Review the key whole-class and drill any item where 'did + past verb' ('Did she called?') appeared.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. Have / tried · 2. happened · 3. the main library is · 4. costs · 5. wrote · 6. did / speak

Practice B: 1. Could you tell me where you parked your car? · 2. Do you know when the exam results will be ready? / Could you tell me when the exam results will be ready? · 3. Do you know where the nearest pharmacy is? · 4. answers vary (e.g. 'What field are you thinking of moving into?' / 'What made you decide to make a change?') · 5. Did she call you after the interview? · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'How long have you been studying English?')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A3 'the library is' — embedded statement word order after 'Could you tell me where…'.

• A5 'wrote' (subject question — 'Who' is the author) vs A6 'did / write' (object question — 'Hamlet' is the object).

• B1 and B2 accept any polite opener ('Could you tell me…', 'Do you know…', 'Would you mind telling me…') provided the embedded clause uses statement order ('…what time the pharmacy closes', '…if/whether there is a cash machine near here').

• B4 is open — credit any two follow-up questions that react directly to passing a driving test.

• B6 accepts any accurate 'How long have you been…' or 'How long does it take…' question.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud with a confident student, pointing out how Speaker A opens with an indirect question ('Could you tell me how you usually spend…?') and follows up on Speaker B's hiking detail.

• Run the three-minute pair interview (3 minutes per partner, then swap): forbid single-sentence topic jumps and require at least two content follow-ups per topic.

• Ask two learners to share the most surprising detail they discovered about their partner.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: Could you tell me how you usually spend a free Friday morning? B: I usually go for a long walk in the hills outside town. A: Really? Who do you usually go with, and how long does the trail take? B: I go with my older brother — it takes about two hours, and we stop for tea on the way back. How about you?

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Guide the class through the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): shadow-read the five polite openers and transform three direct questions into indirect ones without pausing.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): demonstrate negative questions for surprise ('Didn't we meet at the conference?'), short echo questions ('You're moving to Herat? Really?'), and conversational question tags ('It's a great course, isn't it?').

• Have pairs practice a 30-second exchange that includes one echo question and one question tag.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Have each learner choose one starter statement from Part 7 (or invent a true one) and spend 20 seconds thinking of two interesting details they can share when asked.

• Run the two-minute unscripted conversation: Partner A says the opening sentence, and Partner B keeps the conversation alive for two full minutes using reactions, direct/indirect questions, and follow-ups — then swap roles.

• Uncover the printed Model response, compare how both speakers shared the floor, and highlight one strong follow-up question heard in the room.

Student Book model response:

A: I almost missed my flight last week.
B: Really? What happened?
A: The main road to the airport was closed, so I reached the check-in desk twenty minutes before boarding. Do you travel often, or do you prefer staying close to home?
B: I fly for work a few times a year. Could you tell me how you managed to get through security in time?
A: One of the staff saw my boarding pass and took me to the front of the queue. Have you ever missed a connection?
B: Not a flight, but I missed the last bus from Herat once. How did you feel when you finally sat down on the plane?

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four Partner listening checklist targets: accurate direct question auxiliaries, embedded statement order in indirect questions, genuine content follow-ups, and balanced turn-taking.

• If a pair gets stuck, point them silently to the reaction stems on the board so they can keep the conversation moving without switching into their first language.

• Record two examples of inverted indirect questions anonymously for the end-of-lesson board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs ask the same question in two ways (direct for a friend, indirect for a professor) and fire three natural follow-up questions at a partner's statement.

• Have learners complete the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 3 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the two word-order frames on the board visible during Pair Speaking so developing speakers can visually check Subject + Verb order after 'Could you tell me…'.

• Give hesitant listeners a simple two-step formula: 'Repeat one key word + ask Why or How' (e.g., 'A new dish? What did you make?').

• If a learner keeps saying 'Did she called?', run a 30-second oral drill ('Did you go / Did she see / Did they finish') before Part 7.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Challenge confident speakers to use at least one negative question ('Didn't you…?') and one question tag ('…isn't it?') naturally during their Part 5 interview.

• Ask stronger pairs to compare how they would ask the same sensitive question (e.g., asking for a deadline extension) to a close colleague, a department head, and an external client.

• During Real Talk, encourage confident speakers to use 'I was wondering whether…' for their indirect question.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'Could you tell me where is the station?' → 'Could you tell me where the station is?' — Fix: circle the subject ('the station') and place the verb ('is') after it.

• 'Did she called you last night?' → 'Did she call you last night?' — Fix: remind learners that 'did' already carries the past tense, so the main verb stays in the base form.

• 'Who did break the cup?' → 'Who broke the cup?' — Fix: when 'Who' is the person doing the action, no 'did' is used (unless stressing a contradiction).

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two interview prompts per partner in Part 5.

• Practise the polite openers in Part 6 together and set the question-tag / negative-question items as a short take-home task.

• Run a 90-second Real Talk round per partner and finish with the closed-book recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner asks you or a classmate one polite indirect question before leaving the room.

• Carry the three-step follow-up habit (React → Ask a detail → Invite back) into every Pair Speaking activity for the rest of the course.

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 3 in Appendix 1 for review before Review Test 1.

• Feedback focus: Start your post-task feedback by quoting one follow-up question from the room that showed genuine listening. Then put two anonymous indirect-question word-order slips on the board and let pairs fix them together.

LESSON 4 · MODAL VERBS FOR REAL-LIFE SITUATIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: express ability, advice, obligation, permission, possibility and certainty at the right strength

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Select modal verbs that match the exact social strength of a situation — advice, obligation, absence of obligation, prohibition, permission, and polite requests.

• Use modals of deduction ('must be', 'might/could be', 'can't be') and past deduction ('must have been', 'might have missed', 'can't have known') to reason from evidence.

• Resolve a delicate workplace or everyday problem in a two-minute role-play using polite requests, logical deductions, and constructive advice.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners clearly separate prohibition ('mustn't') from lack of obligation ('don't have to') and negative deduction ('can't be')

✓ polite requests with 'Would you mind + verb-ing?' are formed and answered accurately ('No, not at all')

✓ in the Pair Speaking and Real Talk tasks, speakers soften advice and requests rather than issuing blunt commands

Before class begins:

• Draw two simple scales on the board: (1) OBLIGATION & ADVICE: must / have to → should / ought to → might want to / could; (2) DEDUCTION FROM EVIDENCE: must be (95% sure Yes) → might/could be (possible) → can't be (95% sure No).

• Write the classic contrast pair 'You mustn't come tomorrow' vs 'You don't have to come tomorrow' on the board for Part 1.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two situations in Part 1 aloud ('You must solve this problem today' vs 'We might want to look at this problem today'; 'You mustn't come in tomorrow' vs 'You don't have to come in tomorrow') and discuss who has a relaxing Saturday!

• Give pairs 90 seconds to answer the two personal hook prompts (giving advice to a friend with a sore throat before a presentation, and asking a busy director to leave thirty minutes early).

• Show how modals act as the volume control of English — letting speakers sound diplomatic, confident, or firm without changing the topic.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Obligation, prohibition, and advice): contrast internal/strong obligation ('must') and external rules ('have to') with the crucial split between 'mustn't' (forbidden) and 'don't have to' (optional).

• Teach Rule 2 (Deduction from evidence): use clues in the classroom ('Her coat is on the chair, so she must be in the building'; 'The lights are off, so they can't be in a meeting') and show how past deduction uses 'modal + have + past participle'.

• Teach Rule 3 (Polite requests and offers): drill 'Would you mind + verb-ing?' and its natural green-light answer ('No, not at all / Of course not').

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'You mustn't pay' vs 'You don't have to pay' — which one means the ticket is free? ('You don't have to pay.')

• 'His car isn't in the car park — he (mustn't / can't) be in the office.' Which modal expresses logical impossibility? ('can't be'.)

• If someone asks 'Would you mind opening the window?' and you are happy to open it, do you say 'Yes' or 'No, not at all'? ('No, not at all' — meaning 'I do not mind'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, the three-way split between 'mustn't', 'don't have to', and 'can't be'; second, the difference between general past ability ('could') and a specific hard-won past success ('was able to / managed to').

• Have pairs test each other on the board scales: one partner names a situation ('It's a hospital no-smoking zone'), and the other picks the exact modal.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes for Practice A (6 items) individually, then check in pairs — ask learners to justify A3 ('can't' for logical impossibility) vs A4 ('mustn't' for prohibition).

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: have learners perform B1 and B5 aloud as natural mini-exchanges and explain the deduction repair in B4.

• Confirm the key whole-class and chorally practise 'Would you mind closing the window?' — 'No, not at all.'

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. should · 2. could · 3. must · 4. mustn't · 5. might / may / could · 6. Would / opening

Practice B: 1. Could you open the window, please? / Would you mind opening the window? · 2. She must be at home. · 3. He might have missed the early train. / He may / could have missed the early train. · 4. He can't be at home — all his lights are off. · 5. No, not at all. / Of course not — take your time. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'You should drink some water and rest your eyes. You might also want to step outside for some fresh air.')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A3 'can't' — evidence ('just had a huge lunch') points to logical impossibility now.

• A4 'mustn't' — touching live wires is dangerous and strictly forbidden.

• A5 accepts 'might', 'may', or 'could' — 'I'm not sure' signals 50% possibility.

• B3 accepts 'might have missed / may have missed / could have missed' — past possibility.

• B4 'He can't be at home' — repairs 'mustn't be' because dark windows are evidence for a deduction, not a rule.

• B5 'No, not at all. / Of course not. I'll turn it down right away.' — confirms willingness politely.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how the two committee members weigh options using 'should', 'mustn't', 'could', and 'might'.

• Give pairs four minutes to negotiate the workplace budget decision in Part 5 (weekend trip vs communication workshop vs coffee machine) and agree on one final choice.

• Have two pairs announce their final decision and reasoning to the room.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: I think we should choose the communication workshop because the whole team will benefit from it all year. B: That's true, though we mustn't ignore how tired everyone has been lately — a trip could boost morale. A: What if we book a half-day workshop and use the remaining budget for a team lunch on Friday? B: That might be the best compromise — the director ought to approve that easily.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): point to three real clues in or outside the classroom and have pairs make one 'must be', one 'might be', and one 'can't be' deduction aloud.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise past deductions ('They must have got stuck in traffic'), softened professional advice ('You might want to back up those files', 'It might be worth checking…'), and 'would' for polite distance ('I'd suggest…').

• Have each learner rewrite one blunt 'You must…' statement into a diplomatic workplace suggestion.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Have pairs choose one of the three realistic situations in Part 7 (delayed laptop repair, noisy hotel room before an exam, or a teammate who missed a deadline) and spend 30 seconds planning their opening request, deduction, and solution.

• Run a two-minute unscripted role-play (1 minute per role, then swap to a second situation) while listening for the four checklist items.

• Uncover the Model response, highlight how it layers 'I was wondering if you could…', 'It must be a busy week…', and 'Could we either… or should I…?', and have pairs try one upgraded turn.

Student Book model response:

Client: Good morning — I was wondering if I could speak to someone about my textbook order. It was due on Tuesday, and it still hasn't arrived.
Professional: I'm very sorry about that. You must be frustrated, especially with classes starting this week. Let me check the tracking number… Ah, it looks as if the parcel was sent to the wrong district depot.
Client: In that case, could I possibly have it delivered tomorrow? I have to teach until four, so it might need to arrive in the evening.
Professional: That should be possible. We could book an evening courier slot for you, or I could have the main bookshop hold a fresh copy for you to collect today. Which would you prefer?

How to guide and assess this task:

• Evaluate role-plays using the four Partner listening checklist criteria: soft request opener, accurate present/past deduction, constructive advice ('should / ought to / could'), and a clear agreed action.

• Judge politeness by grammatical choice and tone rather than accent or speed.

• Note any confusion between 'mustn't' and 'can't be' or between 'could' and 'was able to' for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have learners complete the two oral recall checks in Part 8 (explaining why 'The office is dark, so he mustn't be there' is wrong, and making one polite request plus one past deduction).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and remind them that Review Test 1 follows this lesson.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Leave the two board scales visible during Pair Speaking and Real Talk so learners can visually pick one modal from each scale during their conversation.

• Offer three ready-to-use role-play frames on the board: 'I was wondering if you could…' · 'There must be…' · 'Perhaps we could…'

• If learners say 'Would you mind to help me?', chorally drill 'mind helping / mind waiting / mind checking' for 20 seconds before Part 7.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to include at least one past deduction ('You must have been…' or 'They might have forgotten…') naturally in both Part 5 and Part 7.

• Ask stronger pairs to practise diplomatic disagreement in their budget negotiation using 'That's a fair point, though we might want to consider…' and 'Wouldn't it be safer to…?'

• Have early finishers compare the tone of 'You must finish this by Friday', 'You need to finish this by Friday', and 'We ought to have this ready by Friday'.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'He mustn't be at home — the lights are off.' → 'He can't be at home.' — Fix: 'mustn't' is for rules; 'can't' is for logical deductions.

• 'Would you mind to open the door?' → 'Would you mind opening the door?' — Fix: 'mind' is always followed by the -ing form.

• 'The fire spread quickly, but everyone could escape.' → '…everyone was able to / managed to escape.' — Fix: for one specific past achievement, use 'was able to' or 'managed to' in affirmative sentences.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; give pairs 3 minutes for the budget decision in Part 5.

• Do the classroom deduction drill in Part 6 together and assign the softened workplace rewrites as homework.

• Run one role-play scenario in Part 7 (1 minute per partner) and finish with the Part 8 recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner gives one logical deduction about something in the room and one polite request.

• Remind learners that Review Test 1 (covering Lessons 1–4) can now be completed in class (20 minutes) or as a timed self-check before Lesson 5.

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 4 in Appendix 1 for review.

• Feedback focus: Praise pairs who resolved their Part 7 complaint calmly using soft modals ('Could we…', 'might want to…'). Then put two anonymous modal slips on the board and let the class repair them together.

LESSON 5 · CONDITIONALS FOR DECISIONS AND POSSIBILITIES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: talk about consequences, alternatives and hypothetical situations accurately

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Build accurate zero, first, second, third, and mixed conditional sentences in natural speech.

• Choose the conditional pattern that matches whether a situation is a real future possibility (first), an imaginary present scenario (second), or an unchangeable past event (third/mixed).

• Weigh a complex real-life decision in a one-minute talk using at least three conditional types.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners use the present simple (not 'will') inside ordinary future if-clauses ('If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay inside')

✓ learners keep 'would' and 'would have' in the main result clause rather than inside the if-clause

✓ in the Real Talk Challenge, speakers combine a first conditional, a second conditional, and a third or mixed conditional coherently

Before class begins:

• Write four clear labels across the board: REAL HABIT/FACT (Zero) · REAL FUTURE PLAN (First) · IMAGINARY NOW (Second) · UNREAL PAST & PRESENT ECHO (Third / Mixed).

• Write the three airport sentences from Part 1 on the board so learners can see the shift from real plan to imaginary present to past regret.

Lesson step
