Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the three airport sentences in Part 1 aloud ('If we leave at six, we'll catch the early flight' / 'If we had a car, we wouldn't need a taxi' / 'If we had left at six, we wouldn't have missed the flight') and identify which speaker still has a chance to catch the plane.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to answer the two personal hook questions (a real plan for this weekend vs an imaginary change to their city or schedule).

• Explain that conditionals are not five disconnected rules — they are one system for moving from real possibilities to hypothetical thinking.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Zero and First conditionals for real situations): highlight that ordinary future if-clauses take the present simple ('If the train arrives on time, I'll call you'), while noting that 'will' can appear in an if-clause only when expressing polite willingness or refusal.

• Teach Rule 2 (Second conditional for imaginary present/future): show how English steps one tense back ('If + past simple → would + base verb') to signal distance from present reality, including the classic advice frame 'If I were you, I'd…'.

• Teach Rule 3 (Third and Mixed conditionals): contrast a purely past regret ('If I had known, I would have told you') with a past cause that shapes right now ('If she had taken that job, she would live in Herat now').

• Teach Rule 4 (Natural connectors beyond 'if'): practise 'unless' (= if not), 'as long as / provided that', and 'in case'.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'If it will rain tomorrow, we'll cancel the picnic' — how do we repair the if-clause for an ordinary future condition? ('If it rains tomorrow…')

• 'If I would have known your number, I would have called' — where does 'had' belong? ('If I had known…')

• Rewrite 'If you don't hurry, you'll be late' using 'unless'. ('Unless you hurry, you'll be late' — no 'don't' after 'unless'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Compare the two tables in Part 3: first, First vs Second Conditional ('If I have time tomorrow' vs 'If I had more free time'); second, Third vs Mixed Conditional ('wouldn't have missed the flight then' vs 'would be in Istanbul right now').

• Ask pairs to explain in their own words what changes when 'would have + participle' shifts to 'would + base verb (now)'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, then compare in pairs and read each sentence aloud with natural contractions ('I'd', 'wouldn't have').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners transform B1–B4 aloud and share their personal second-conditional answers for B5 and B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class, pausing on B4 ('If I had known…') to reinforce why 'would have' never belongs inside the if-clause.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. heat / boils · 2. rains / will cancel (or: 'll cancel) · 3. were / would apologise · 4. had left / wouldn't have missed · 5. knew / would call · 6. will go / stays

Practice B: 1. Unless you register before Friday, you can't attend the seminar. · 2. If he had checked the timetable, he wouldn't have missed the ferry. · 3. If she had saved enough money last year, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy the car now. · 4. If I have free time tonight, I will review the vocabulary. · 5. answers vary (e.g. 'If I were you, I wouldn't resign until I had a signed offer in hand.') · 6. answers vary

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A3 'were / would apologise' — 'If I were you' is standard in careful spoken and written English; note that 'was' is heard in casual speech, as explained in Rule 2.

• A4 'had known / would have visited' — third conditional for an unchangeable past situation.

• B2 'If he had studied, he wouldn't have failed' — remind learners to drop 'so' when combining two clauses with 'if'.

• B3 'If I had slept last night, I wouldn't be tired now' — mixed conditional linking a past cause to a present state.

• B5 and B6 are open — credit any well-formed second conditional advice or imaginary scenario.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how a chain story builds from third conditional to mixed conditional to second conditional advice.

• Run the four-minute chain game in pairs using the three starter prompts in Part 5: each partner picks up the result of the previous sentence and turns it into the next 'If…' condition.

• Have two pairs perform their most creative four-sentence chain for the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: If I had woken up on time this morning, I would have caught the seven o'clock bus. B: And if you had caught that bus, you would have arrived at the café before the rain started. A: True — and if I hadn't walked through the rain, my notes wouldn't be wet right now! B: If I were you, I'd keep a spare umbrella in your bag from now on.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Guide the class through the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs say one true sentence for each of the five conditional types and practise the spoken contractions ('If I'd known…', 'She'd help if she could').

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): introduce formal inverted conditionals ('Should you need…', 'Were we to…', 'Had I known…'), 'But for your help…', and conversational 'Suppose / What if…?' openers.

• Have pairs transform one third conditional from Practice B into a formal 'Had I…' sentence.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to plan their one-minute talk on a major life or career decision (or a past turning point), jotting down keywords for one first conditional, one second conditional, and one third or mixed conditional.

• Partners take turns speaking for one full minute while the listener ticks the four criteria in the Partner listening checklist.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it moves from 'If I pass the entrance exam…' to 'If the tuition were lower…' to 'If my mentor hadn't encouraged me…', and have learners refine one sentence from their talk.

Student Book model response:

If we invest this grant in staff training, our whole team will improve their teaching skills, and students will feel the benefit within a month. Buying new computers would look impressive at first, but if I were leading the committee, I would put people ahead of hardware every time. In fact, if we had set aside a small training fund last year, we wouldn't be facing such a steep learning curve with the new curriculum right now. Provided that we schedule the workshops before the new term starts, training is by far the smartest choice.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four checklist items during Part 7: a real future condition (first), a hypothetical present condition (second), a past/mixed reflection (third/mixed), and natural linking.

• Accept any coherent personal decision or turning-point topic.

• Collect two anonymous examples of 'if + would' or 'unless + don't' for the end-of-class board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral retrieval tasks in Part 8 (naming all five conditional types with examples and turning a real past mistake into a third + mixed conditional).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and point anyone who hesitated to Formula Book Card 5.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the four-column board timeline visible so developing speakers can match the time (Future / Now / Past / Past→Now) before speaking.

• Write the third-conditional rhythm on the board as a two-beat chant: 'If I'd KNOWN — I would've TOLD you.'

• If a learner mixes up second and third conditionals, ask simply: 'Are we imagining right now, or looking back at yesterday?'

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Challenge confident speakers to include one formal inverted conditional ('Had I known…' or 'Should the committee approve…') during Part 6 and Part 7.

• Encourage stronger pairs to open their Part 5 chain questions with 'Suppose…' or 'Assuming that…' and use 'provided that' or 'in case' in their responses.

• Ask early finishers to explain the difference between 'I'll take an umbrella if it rains' and 'I'll take an umbrella in case it rains' (preparation beforehand).

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'If it will rain tomorrow, we'll stay home.' → 'If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.' — Fix: ordinary future conditions take the present simple after 'if'.

• 'If I would have known, I would have helped.' → 'If I had known, I would have helped.' — Fix: keep 'would have' in the result clause only.

• 'Unless you don't start now, you won't finish.' → 'Unless you start now, you won't finish.' — Fix: 'unless' already means 'if not'.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two chain rounds in Part 5 instead of three.

• Practice spoken contractions in Part 6 in class and assign the formal inverted conditionals as written homework.

• Run one 60-second Real Talk turn per partner followed by the closed-book recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner produces one third or mixed conditional about their week before leaving.

• Flag Formula Book Card 5 in Appendix 1 as a core revision card for Review Test 2 (after Lesson 8).

• Remind learners how Lesson 6 (Wishes and Regrets) will build directly on today's 'one step back in time' rule.

• Feedback focus: During the chain game and Real Talk, let speakers finish their thought before addressing any tense slip. Afterwards, write two anonymous 'if + would' sentences on the board and have pairs repair them aloud.

LESSON 6 · WISHES, REGRETS, AND HYPOTHETICAL SITUATIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: express preferences, dissatisfaction, regrets and imagined alternatives naturally

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Express present wishes ('I wish I had…'), past regrets ('I wish I had taken…'), and frustrations with changeable behaviour ('I wish you would…') using accurate verb forms.

• Express personal and interpersonal preferences naturally using 'would rather', 'prefer', and 'It's (high) time + past simple'.

• Deliver a thoughtful one-minute reflection on a past regret, a present wish, and practical advice for a younger learner.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners accurately distinguish 'wish + past simple' (present wish) from 'wish + past perfect' (past regret)

✓ learners switch cleanly between 'I'd rather stay' (same subject + base verb) and 'I'd rather you stayed' (different subject + past simple)

✓ in the Real Talk Challenge, speakers combine one past regret, one present wish, and one piece of advice naturally

Before class begins:

• Write three clear headers on the board: WISH ABOUT NOW (wish + past simple) · REGRET ABOUT THE PAST (wish + had + participle) · WANT SOMETHING TO CHANGE (wish + would + base verb).

• Write the two contrast pairs from Part 1 on the board ('I wish I spoke Arabic' vs 'I wish I had learned Arabic at school'; 'I'd rather stay home' vs 'I'd rather you stayed home').

Lesson step

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

Say It with Greater Precision

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two sentence pairs in Part 1 aloud and explain which speaker is wishing about today and which is looking back with regret at school days.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to complete the three honest personal stems in Part 1 ('One skill I wish I had right now…', 'One decision from the past few years I wish I had made differently…', and 'One habit I'd rather change this month…').

• Connect today's rule to Lesson 5: just like unreal conditionals, wishes and regrets step one tense back from reality.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Present wishes: 'wish / if only + past simple' and 'wish + could') and Rule 2 (Past regrets: 'wish / if only + past perfect' and 'wish + would' for annoying habits or situations we want someone else to change).

• Emphasise the golden rule for 'wish + would': we never say 'I wish I would…' about ourselves.

• Teach Rule 3 ('would rather' and 'It's high time'): contrast same-subject 'I'd rather walk' with different-subject 'I'd rather you didn't mention this', and drill 'It's high time we started.'

• Teach Rule 4 ('prefer' and 'as if / as though'): compare literal 'It looks as if it's going to rain' with unreal 'He talks as if he knew everything.'

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'I wish I have more time today' — why is 'have' wrong here, and what is the fix? ('I wish I had more time' — present wishes step back to the past simple.)

• 'I'd rather you don't tell anyone' — how do we fix the verb after 'you'? ('I'd rather you didn't tell anyone' — different subject takes the past simple.)

• Can we say 'I wish I would be taller'? (No — 'would' is only for changeable behaviour by someone else; say 'I wish I were/was taller'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, Present Wish vs Past Regret vs Complaint ('I wish I knew' / 'I wish I had known' / 'I wish he would reply'); second, the three patterns with 'It's time' ('It's time to leave' / 'It's time for us to leave' / 'It's high time we left').

• Have pairs test each other by calling out a time cue ('right now!' or 'last year!') and having their partner transform 'I wish I…' accordingly.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, then check in pairs — pay special attention to A4 ('It's high time we made…') and A6 ('as if he were/was…').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners transform B1–B5 aloud and share their true present wish and past regret for B6.

• Review the key whole-class and chorally drill B3 ('I wish I had more free time') and B4 ('It's time we went home').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. knew · 2. hadn't said · 3. owned · 4. made · 5. didn't tell · 6. were (or: was in informal speech)

Practice B: 1. I wish I had studied harder at school. · 2. I'd rather you didn't smoke near the doorway. · 3. I wish I had more free time this semester. · 4. It's already midnight — it's time we went home. · 5. reading / watching · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'He burst through the door out of breath, as if he had run all the way from the station.')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A2 'had taken' — 'last year' signals a past regret, requiring 'wish + past perfect'.

• A4 'made' — 'It's high time + subject + past simple' expresses that the action is already overdue.

• A6 accepts 'were' (traditional subjunctive) or 'was' (informal speech) after 'as if he…'.

• B3 'I wish I had more free time' — repairs 'have' to 'had' for an unreal present wish.

• B5 'reading / watching' — parallel -ing forms after 'prefer X to Y'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how Speaker A expresses a real frustration with 'I wish I had…' and 'I wish I could…', and Speaker B responds empathetically with 'It's high time…' and 'If I were you…'.

• Run the four-minute Pair Speaking activity: Partner A shares a real frustration from one of the four life areas (schedule, study/work space, technology, or travel/health), and Partner B responds with empathy and practical suggestions — then swap roles.

• Invite two pairs to share their most realistic exchange with the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: I really wish I had more quiet time in the mornings — my commute is so noisy that I arrive at work already tired. B: I know the feeling! Have you tried taking the earlier bus, or would you rather not wake up at six? A: I wish I could, but I have to drop my younger brother at school first. B: Then it's high time you got a good pair of noise-cancelling headphones — if I were you, I'd listen to calm music on the way.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): each learner says two true sentences about right now ('I wish I had/could…') and two about the past ('I wish I had…').

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise 'If only…!' for stronger emotional weight, polite workplace 'I'd rather you didn't…', 'What I should have done was…', and 'as though nothing had happened'.

• Ask pairs to compare when 'I wish you would…' sounds like a fair request and when a softer request ('Would you mind…?') is wiser.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to jot down keywords for their one-minute reflection: (1) a past regret ('I wish I had…'), (2) a present wish ('I wish I had/could…'), and (3) practical advice for someone younger ('If I were you…' / 'It's high time…').

• Partners speak for one full minute each while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, notice how it links 'I wish I had started speaking out loud from the very first week', 'Today, I wish I had more opportunities…', and 'It's high time we stopped treating mistakes as failures', and have learners polish one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

I wish I had taken spoken English seriously during my first two years at university — I wasted countless classes staying silent because I was afraid of making small grammar slips. Even today, I sometimes wish I could express complex technical ideas as effortlessly as my mentor does. But that regret taught me something valuable: fluency only grows when you use the language out loud. It's high time we stopped treating mistakes as failures. If I were advising a first-year student today, I'd tell them to record themselves speaking for two minutes every week — within a month, you can hear the difference.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four checklist items during Part 7: accurate past regret ('wish + had + participle'), accurate present wish ('wish + past simple / could'), natural advice or urgency ('It's high time…'), and a reflective, conversational tone.

• Respond to the speaker's real meaning first before noting any form slips.

• Put two anonymous slips (typically 'wish + present' or 'wish + past simple for yesterday') on the board for a brisk whole-class repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (one present wish + one past regret, and two 'would rather' sentences with same vs different subjects).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 6 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the three board headers visible so developing speakers can check whether their wish is about NOW (past simple) or THEN (past perfect) before speaking.

• Offer simple sentence starters: 'Looking back, I wish I had…' · 'Right now, I wish I could…' · 'It's high time we…'

• If a learner confuses B1 and B3, have them say 'Today I wish I knew' and 'Yesterday I wish I had known' back-to-back three times.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Invite confident speakers to include 'What I should have done was…' or 'as though nothing had happened' in their Part 5 and Part 7 turns.

• Challenge stronger pairs to reframe a blunt workplace complaint ('I wish you would stop sending late emails') into a diplomatic preference ('I'd rather we agreed on a cut-off time for emails').

• Ask early finishers to contrast 'It's time to leave' (neutral schedule) with 'It's high time we left' (overdue and urgent).

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'I wish I have more time.' → 'I wish I had more time.' — Fix: unreal present wishes always step one tense back to the past simple.

• 'I wish I went to the seminar yesterday.' → 'I wish I had gone to the seminar yesterday.' — Fix: past regrets require 'had + past participle'.

• 'It's time we will go home.' → 'It's time we went home.' — Fix: never use 'will' after 'It's (high) time + subject'.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two life areas in Part 5 instead of four.

• Practise the now-vs-then wish drill in Part 6 in class and assign the diplomatic workplace rewrites as homework.

• Run one 60-second Real Talk reflection per partner and close with the Part 8 oral check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one past regret ('I wish I had…') and one preference ('I'd rather…') before leaving.

• Remind learners that wishes and 'It's high time' appear directly in Review Test 2 (items A2 and A6).

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 6 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Acknowledge the honesty and thoughtfulness of learners' reflections first; then use two anonymous board examples to reinforce the 'wish + past simple (now)' vs 'wish + had + participle (then)' contrast.

LESSON 7 · COMPARISONS BEYOND THE BASICS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: compare clearly and support comparisons with reasons

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Form accurate comparatives, superlatives, and equality structures ('as…as', 'not nearly as…as', 'twice as…as') across adjectives and adverbs.

• Use degree modifiers ('far', 'much', 'a great deal', 'slightly', 'by far') and 'the + comparative, the + comparative' patterns to make comparisons precise and persuasive.

• Deliver a persuasive one-minute recommendation comparing two real options with at least three modified comparisons and clear reasons.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ zero double comparatives ('more better', 'more taller') and zero 'then/than' confusions in practice and speaking

✓ every comparison in Pair Speaking and Real Talk is supported by a concrete reason ('because…')

✓ speakers use at least two degree modifiers ('far more…', 'slightly cheaper', 'by far the best…') and one 'the more…, the more…' pattern

Before class begins:

• Write the degree-modifier scale on the board: BIG DIFFERENCE ('far / much / a great deal / a lot') · SMALL DIFFERENCE ('slightly / a little / a bit') · SUPERLATIVE SPOTLIGHT ('by far / easily / one of the most…').

• Write the two laptop recommendations from Part 1 on the board so learners can see the contrast between a flat opinion ('good and cheap') and a persuasive comparison ('far lighter… and the battery lasts nearly twice as long').

Lesson step

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

5

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

Say It with Greater Precision

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two laptop recommendations in Part 1 aloud and identify the exact words that make Speaker B's recommendation convincing.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to compare the two hook topics aloud (studying early in the morning vs late at night; learning in a classroom vs studying online alone) using a 'because' reason for each choice.

• Establish today's core principle: a bare comparison states an opinion, but a modified comparison plus a reason persuades a listener.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Comparatives and superlatives: short vs long words and irregular forms 'good/better/best', 'bad/worse/worst', 'far/further/furthest'), reminding learners never to double up with 'more + -er'.

• Teach Rule 2 (Equality, multiples, and double comparatives): drill 'just as effective as', 'twice as fast as', and the cause-and-effect rhythm of 'The more you practise, the more confident you become.'

• Teach Rule 3 (Degree modifiers): show how placing 'far', 'much', 'slightly', or 'by far' before a comparison tells the listener the exact size of the difference.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'She is more taller than her sister' — what is the error, and how do we repair it? ('She is taller' or 'much taller' — never combine 'more' with '-er'.)

• 'She speaks English more fluent than before' — why do we need 'more fluently'? (Because it describes how she speaks — an adverb, not a noun.)

• Where does 'twice' or 'three times' sit in an 'as…as' comparison? (Right before the first 'as': 'twice as expensive as'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two tables in Part 3: first, Comparative (two choices) vs Superlative (standout in a group); second, how adding degree modifiers and multiples ('far cheaper', 'almost as fast as', 'three times as many') sharpens vague statements.

• Have pairs take one plain sentence ('Bus travel is cheaper than train travel') and say it aloud in three different strengths ('slightly cheaper', 'far cheaper', 'not nearly as expensive as').

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking that A2 includes 'the worst' and A4 uses the adverb comparative 'more beautifully'.

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners transform B1, repair B2 and B5, and speak their full reason-backed comparisons for B3, B4, and B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class and spotlight why adverbs ending in '-ly' take 'more' ('speaks more fluently', not 'more fluent').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. shorter · 2. the worst · 3. more / faster · 4. more confidently · 5. as / as · 6. most talented

Practice B: 1. The new battery lasts twice as long as the old one. · 2. My younger brother is taller than me now. · 3. Practising with a partner is far better than studying alone because you have to respond in real time. (answers vary) · 4. answers vary (e.g. 'The more often you speak in class, the more confident you feel.') · 5. This dictionary is much clearer than my old one. · 6. answers vary

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A2 'the worst' — superlative of 'bad' with 'of my life'.

• A4 'more beautifully' — adverb comparative modifying 'sings'.

• B1 'This phone is twice as expensive as that one' — multiplier precedes the first 'as'.

• B3 and B6 are open — credit any accurate comparison using 'far/much/a lot + comparative + because…' and any three-city comparison using both comparative and superlative forms.

• B5 repairs 'then' (time) to 'than' (comparison).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how the two partners weigh online vs classroom courses and reach a joint blended-learning recommendation.

• Give pairs four minutes to debate one of the four decision topics in Part 5 and agree on a joint recommendation using at least three modified comparisons and one 'The more…, the more…' sentence.

• Have two pairs present their joint recommendation in 30 seconds to the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: For our team, an in-person course is far more effective than a self-paced online course because people actually practise speaking together. B: That's true, though online modules are much more flexible for colleagues who travel. A: What if we combine them? The more people review the grammar online at home, the more time we'll have for live speaking in class. B: Agreed — a blended course is by far the smartest option for our budget.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs practise the irregular forms ('better/best', 'worse/worst', 'further/furthest') and make three true comparisons about their week with 'far', 'slightly', and 'just as…as'.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): introduce 'by far the most… / the single most…', concessive comparisons ('While Option A is slightly cheaper, Option B is far more reliable'), and data-framing openers ('Compared with five years ago, …').

• Have each learner build one concessive comparison ('While…, …') about their city or work.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to choose one pair of options in Part 7 and jot down three comparison keywords plus a concrete reason for each.

• Partners take turns speaking for one full minute to persuade their listener while the listener checks the four items in the Partner listening checklist.

• Uncover the Model response, notice how it combines 'While studying alone at home is slightly more convenient…', 'far more effective because…', 'The more you interact…', and 'by far the most enjoyable way…', and have learners upgrade one of their own comparisons.

Student Book model response:

In my view, early childhood is the easiest age to pick up natural pronunciation, because young children imitate sounds far more effortlessly than adults and are much less afraid of making mistakes. However, when it comes to using one hour a day as an adult learner, deliberate speaking practice is by far the most valuable investment you can make. Speaking aloud with a partner is twice as effective as silent review because you get immediate feedback when a sentence is unclear. Compared with memorizing word lists alone, real conversation builds habits that last — and the more regularly you speak, the more natural your grammar becomes.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four Partner listening checklist targets: modified comparative ('far/much/slightly'), superlative or equality pattern ('by far the most…' / 'not nearly as…as'), 'The more…, the more…', and a clear 'because' reason for every comparison.

• Remind listeners that a comparison without a reason does not count toward the target.

• Jot down any adjective-vs-adverb slips or 'more + -er' slips for the three-minute board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral retrieval tasks in Part 8 (one 'far + comparative' sentence, one 'not nearly as…as' sentence, one 'The more…, the more…' sentence, and ranking three cities or skills with superlatives).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 7 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the degree-modifier scale visible on the board so developing speakers can add 'far', 'much', or 'slightly' naturally before every comparative.

• Provide three persuasive sentence frames on the board: 'X is far more… than Y because…' · 'Y is not nearly as… as X' · 'The more we…, the more…'

• If a learner hesitates over short vs long adjectives, have them practise five high-frequency pairs aloud ('cheaper / more expensive', 'faster / more reliable', 'better / more effective').

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to open their recommendation with a concessive comparison ('While X is slightly cheaper in the short term, Y is far better value over time').

• Challenge stronger pairs to include one data-framing comparison ('Compared with last year, … has nearly doubled') during Part 5 or Part 7.

• Ask early finishers to discuss when 'arguably the best' sounds more credible than 'the best' in academic or professional speaking.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'This route is more faster.' → 'This route is much faster.' — Fix: use 'much' or 'far' (never 'more') before an '-er' comparative.

• 'Online courses are cheaper then classroom courses.' → '…cheaper than classroom courses.' — Fix: 'than' compares; 'then' shows time.

• 'The climate here is warmer than London.' → 'The climate here is warmer than London's / than that of London.' — Fix: compare like with like (climate with climate).

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; have pairs debate one topic in Part 5 and state their joint verdict.

• Practise the degree modifiers in Part 6 orally and assign the concessive 'While…, …' sentence as written homework.

• Run one 60-second persuasion turn per partner in Part 7 and finish with the Part 8 recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one persuasive comparison with 'far' or 'by far' and a 'because' reason before leaving.

• Point out that Lesson 8 (Linking Ideas and Building Arguments) will combine today's comparisons with contrast and result linkers for full debates.

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 7 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Tick modified comparisons and reasons separately while listening; praise one speaker who used 'While…' or 'The more…, the more…' persuasively, then repair two anonymous slips on the board.

LESSON 8 · LINKING IDEAS AND BUILDING ARGUMENTS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: organise opinions into coherent, well-linked spoken arguments

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Connect ideas accurately using the four core linker families: contrast/concession ('although', 'despite', 'however'), cause ('because', 'because of', 'since'), result ('therefore', 'as a result'), and purpose ('to', 'in order to', 'so that').

• Match each linker to its grammatical partner — a full clause ('although / because + subject + verb') versus a noun phrase or '-ing' form ('despite / because of + noun/-ing').

• Deliver a structured 90-second argument using the four-step skeleton: Point → Reason → Example → Conclusion.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners use 'despite / in spite of + noun/-ing' (never 'despite of') and 'although + subject + verb' accurately

✓ spoken arguments in Pair Speaking and Real Talk follow the four-step skeleton (Point → Reason → Example → Conclusion)

✓ each speaker acknowledges the other side once ('Although…' / 'Despite…') before defending their main position

Before class begins:

• Draw the two grammar-pairing columns on the board: TAKES A FULL CLAUSE (Subject + Verb): 'although / even though / because / since / so that' vs TAKES A NOUN OR -ING: 'despite / in spite of / because of / due to'.

• Write the four-step argument skeleton across the top of the board: 1. POINT → 2. REASON → 3. EXAMPLE → 4. CONCLUSION ('To sum up, …').

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read Speaker A and Speaker B in Part 1 aloud and discuss why Speaker B sounds ready for a university seminar or management meeting even though both speakers share the exact same facts.

• Run the 45-second hook challenge: Partner A speaks on 'Why people learn English' while Partner B counts how many different linking words go beyond 'and', 'but', and 'so'.

• Explain that strong speakers don't just have better ideas — they signpost the relationship between their ideas so the listener can follow effortlessly.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Contrast and concession): write one idea on the board in three packages — 'Although the traffic was heavy, we arrived on time' (clause), 'Despite the heavy traffic, we arrived on time' (noun), and 'The traffic was heavy. However, we arrived on time' (new sentence).

• Emphasise the two classic traps: never say 'despite of', and never put '-ing' directly after 'although' ('Despite being tired…', not 'Although being tired…').

• Teach Rule 2 (Cause, result, and purpose): contrast 'because + clause' with 'because of / due to + noun', and 'to / in order to + verb' with 'so that + subject + can/could'.

• Teach Rule 3 (The four-step argument skeleton) and Rule 4 (Summarizing linkers: 'To sum up', 'All in all', 'Overall', 'In conclusion').

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'Despite of the rain, we walked' — what word must be removed immediately? ('of' — say 'Despite the rain' or 'In spite of the rain'.)

• 'Although the high price, we bought it' — give two different grammatical ways to fix this sentence. ('Despite the high price, we bought it' or 'Although the price was high, we bought it'.)

• What are the four steps of the argument skeleton in order? (Point → Reason → Example → Conclusion.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, packaging the same contrast three ways ('Although…' / 'Despite…' / 'However, …'); second, Clause Linkers vs Noun-Phrase Linkers side by side.

• Run a 45-second oral transformation drill: you say 'Although the course was expensive, it was worth it', and the class transforms it with 'Despite…' and then with 'However, …'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, then compare in pairs — ask learners to explain why A2 requires 'Despite' before 'being exhausted'.

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners combine B1–B2, repair B3 and B5, and speak their three-sentence argument (B4) and closing summary (B6) aloud.

• Confirm the key whole-class, noting that both 'Despite the high cost…' and 'Although the cost was high…' are valid repairs for B3.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. Despite · 2. Despite (followed by -ing; 'Although' needs a subject + verb: 'Although she felt exhausted') · 3. however · 4. so that · 5. As a result · 6. whereas

Practice B: 1. Although the assignment was challenging, every group finished on time. · 2. Despite not being selected the first time, she applied again the following year. / Despite the initial rejection, she applied again. · 3. Despite the high cost, the hospital purchased the new scanner. · 4. answers vary — must include a clear point, a reason, and an example · 5. Despite the rain, the football match continued. / Although it was raining, the football match continued. · 6. answers vary — must close with To sum up / All in all / In conclusion

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A2 'Despite' — followed by the -ing phrase 'being exhausted after a twelve-hour shift'.

• A3 'because of' — followed by the noun phrase 'heavy snow on the mountain pass'.

• B3 accepts either 'Despite the high cost, we bought the equipment' (noun phrase) or 'Although the cost was high, we bought the equipment' (full clause).

• B4 must visibly include all three parts (Point + Reason + Example) on learning a second language.

• B6 is open — credit any coherent summary of the lesson that opens with 'To sum up,' 'All in all,' or 'In conclusion,'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how the two debaters use 'I firmly believe…', 'Although…', 'Despite…', 'However, …', 'Therefore, …', and 'To sum up, …'.

• Have pairs choose one of the three debate motions in Part 5, take opposite sides, and run a four-minute mini-debate (90 seconds per speaker plus a 1-minute joint conclusion).

• Invite two pairs to share their closing summary sentence with the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: I firmly believe that traditional written homework should be replaced by daily recorded speaking practice. B: Although speaking practice is essential, written homework helps learners notice spelling and sentence structure. A: Despite that advantage, most students already spend hours reading and writing in class; as a result, their spoken fluency lags behind. B: However, some learners feel shy recording themselves at home. A: Therefore, teachers can start with short one-minute voice notes. To sum up, combining short daily recordings with a brief weekly written check gives learners the best balance.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): give pairs 60 seconds to repackage 'It was raining hard, but the match continued' in four ways ('Although', 'Despite', 'In spite of being…', and 'However').

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise concessive counter-balance frames ('It is true that…; nevertheless, …' / 'Admittedly, …; even so, …'), clause-commenting ', which…', and 'Not only does this…, but it also…'.

• Have each learner build one 'Admittedly, …; even so, …' sentence about their debate topic.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to choose one claim in Part 7 and jot down four keywords following the argument skeleton: (1) Main claim, (2) Concession ('Although / Despite'), (3) Reason + concrete example, (4) Closing summary.

• Partners take turns speaking for 90 seconds without reading while the listener checks the four items in the Partner listening checklist.

• Uncover the Model response, trace its four skeleton stages ('I firmly believe…', 'This is mainly because…', 'For instance…', 'Although some managers worry…', 'To sum up…'), and have learners tighten one transition in their own talk.

Student Book model response:

I believe what makes a truly effective teacher is clear, honest feedback combined with patience. This is because learners improve fastest when they know exactly what to adjust without feeling discouraged. For instance, my first English instructor corrected our pronunciation habits every day with a warm smile, and as a result our whole class gained confidence within a month. Although entertaining games can make a classroom lively, I would trade entertainment for clear guidance any day. To sum up, a great teacher shows you the next step clearly and makes you believe you can take it.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Evaluate the 90-second talks using the four Partner listening checklist criteria: four-step argument skeleton, accurate contrast linker ('although' + clause or 'despite' + noun/-ing), cause/result linker, and a clear closing summary.

• Judge the talk by structural clarity and linker accuracy rather than personal agreement with the claim.

• Collect two anonymous clause-vs-noun linker slips for the end-of-lesson board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (a 20-second mini-argument on the four-step skeleton and expressing one contrast in three grammatical ways).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and remind them that Review Test 2 (Lessons 1–8) follows this lesson.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep both the Clause vs Noun chart and the four-step Argument Skeleton visible on the board throughout Parts 5 and 7.

• Provide four ready-to-use signpost openers on the board: 'I believe that…' · 'This is mainly because…' · 'For instance, …' · 'To sum up, …'

• If a learner says 'Despite of…' or 'Although + noun', pause after their turn and ask them to point to the Clause vs Noun column on the board to self-correct.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to use 'Admittedly, …; even so, …' or 'It is true that…; nevertheless, …' when handling the counterargument in Part 7.

• Challenge stronger pairs to include one 'Not only does this…, but it also…' inversion or one clause-commenting ', which…' sentence during their mini-debate.

• Ask early finishers to compare the register and punctuation of 'however', 'nevertheless', and 'yet'.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'Despite of the delay, we arrived on time.' → 'Despite the delay… / In spite of the delay…' — Fix: 'despite' never takes 'of'.

• 'Although being tired, she finished the report.' → 'Despite being tired… / Although she was tired…' — Fix: 'although' requires a subject and verb.

• Listing disconnected opinions ('First… Also… Another thing…') — Fix: require the four-step skeleton (Point → Reason → Example → Conclusion) for every opinion turn.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run a 2-minute mini-debate in Part 5.

• Do the four-way contrast repackaging in Part 6 in class and assign the 'Not only…' / 'Admittedly…' sentences as homework.

• Run a 60-second Real Talk argument per partner and close with the Part 8 oral recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner states one contrast idea in two ways — once with 'although' and once with 'despite'.

• Remind learners that Review Test 2 (covering Lessons 1–8) follows this lesson; point them to Formula Book Cards 1–8 in Appendix 1.

• Note that the four-step argument skeleton taught today will be used again in Lessons 15 and 16 and in the Final Assessment speaking task.

• Feedback focus: Praise speakers who clearly signposted their four argument stages ('This is mainly because…', 'For instance…', 'To sum up…'). Then put two anonymous 'although / despite' slips on the board and let pairs repair them in 60 seconds.

LESSON 9 · PASSIVE VOICE IN NATURAL ENGLISH — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 5 — Describe and Explain | Speaking goal: choose between active and passive for the right focus

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Form accurate passive sentences across present, past, present perfect, future, and modal structures by changing the tense of 'be' before the past participle.

• Choose wisely between active and passive voice so the listener's attention lands on the person, object, or result that matters most.

• Deliver a calm, objective 90-second news or workplace briefing using passive structures, one formal reporting structure ('It is said that…' / 'X is expected to…'), and an active closing opinion.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners form passives across at least three tenses without dropping 'be' or misforming past participles

✓ learners keep ordinary personal actions active ('I lost my phone', not 'My phone was lost by me')

✓ in the Real Talk briefing, speakers use at least four passives, one formal reporting frame, and one final active comment

Before class begins:

• Write the core passive formula on the board: RECEIVER + BE (in the right tense) + PAST PARTICIPLE (+ by doer only when informative).

• List the five high-frequency passive tense shapes on the board: 'is/are done' · 'was/were done' · 'has/have been done' · 'will be done' · 'must/can be done'.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two sentence pairs in Part 1 aloud ('Someone stole my bicycle outside the library' vs 'My bicycle was stolen outside the library'; 'Workers built this bridge in 1974' vs 'This bridge was built in 1974') and explain why the second sentence in each pair sounds sharper.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to answer the two hook prompts (naming two things in their city that were built or repaired recently, and describing a product or dish made in their region).

• Explain that the passive is a camera move: we swing the lens from an unknown or obvious doer to the result, the object, or the person affected.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (How the passive works): show how 'be' does all the tense work while the main verb stays a past participle, and have the class read the five tense examples aloud.

• Teach Rule 2 (When to choose the passive — and when to stay active): highlight that we use the passive when the doer is unknown, obvious, or less important than the result, or when we want an objective tone — and we stay active for our own everyday actions.

• Teach Rule 3 (Formal reporting passives): practise the twin patterns 'It is said/believed/expected that + clause' and 'Subject + is said/believed/expected + to + base verb'.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'The bridge was builted in 1980' — what is the correct past participle of 'build'? ('built' — 'The bridge was built in 1980'.)

• 'My keys were lost by me this morning' — why does that sound unnatural, and what should we say instead? ('I lost my keys this morning' — use active voice for your own ordinary actions.)

• Transform 'People say that she speaks five languages' in two ways. ('It is said that she speaks…' and 'She is said to speak…')

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, Active vs Passive camera focus (including why 'I lost my keys' beats 'My keys were lost by me'); second, Personal Active vs Impersonal Reporting Passives.

• Run a quick oral transform: you say 'People expect that the new metro line will open in autumn', and pairs produce both 'It is expected that…' and 'The new metro line is expected to…'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, paying special attention to word order in A5 ('has just been introduced') and the modal passive in A6 ('must be signed').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners transform B1–B3, repair B4 and B5, and share their two-sentence local project update for B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class and spotlight why B5 ('My phone was stolen by me') must be repaired to 'I lost my phone' (or 'My phone was stolen').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. was built · 2. will be announced · 3. is cleaned · 4. was stolen · 5. has just been introduced · 6. be submitted

Practice B: 1. My bicycle has been stolen. · 2. The board made the final decision. · 3. It is said that he is the strongest candidate. / He is said to be the strongest candidate. · 4. The old courthouse was built in 1990. · 5. I lost my phone on the way home. · 6. The main tunnel will be closed tomorrow for maintenance.

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A5 'has just been introduced' — present perfect passive with 'just' placed after 'has'.

• B2 'The board made the decision' — restores the agent ('the board') as the active subject.

• B3 accepts both 'It is said that he is the best surgeon in the city' and 'He is said to be the best surgeon in the city'.

• B5 'I lost my phone' (or 'My phone was stolen') — removes the unnatural self-agent 'by me'.

• B6 is open — credit any two-sentence project description using one past passive and one future passive.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn Newsroom model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how the reporter uses passives and 'It is expected that…' while the editor asks 'Who…?' to trigger an active or 'by…' response.

• Run the four-minute Newsroom briefing in pairs: Partner A (Reporter) delivers three local or workplace updates using passive forms; Partner B (Editor) asks follow-up questions about who was responsible and what will happen next — then swap roles.

• Invite two reporters to share their clearest news item with the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: A new solar power clinic was opened in the northern district yesterday, and twenty local technicians have already been trained to run it. B: That's great news. Who funded the construction? A: The equipment was donated by two regional hospitals, and it is expected that three more clinics will be built next year.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs point to four objects in the classroom and describe each one in a different passive tense.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise conversational 'get' passives ('got promoted', 'got delayed'), past reporting infinitives ('is believed to have started'), and past-participle openings ('Founded in 1998, the institute…').

• Have each learner build one 'Founded / Built / Located in…' opening sentence about a real place.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to jot down keywords for three recent events in their city, school, or workplace (one past event, one recent change, and one future plan).

• Partners take turns delivering their 90-second objective briefing while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist items.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it moves from 'Last month, the main city library was reopened…' to 'has been installed…' to 'It is expected that…' before ending with an active personal opinion, and have learners polish one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

Three important updates have happened around our campus this week. First, a new pedestrian footbridge was opened near the east gate on Monday, so morning traffic has been diverted away from the main walkway. Second, two study rooms on the third floor have been fitted with new lighting and quiet desks. Finally, it is expected that the library hours will be extended during the exam period next month. In my view, the administration should publish the new evening timetable as soon as possible so students can plan their transport home.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four Partner listening checklist criteria: four passive verb forms across at least two tenses, one formal reporting structure, natural 'by' agent choice, and a final active opinion.

• Accept any authentic local, campus, or workplace news items.

• Note any missing forms of 'be' ('The report finished yesterday') or irregular participle slips for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (three passive sentences in different tenses about the classroom and two formal reporting versions of 'People believe that…').

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 9 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the five-tense passive chart visible on the board so developing speakers can check the form of 'be' before speaking.

• Provide three briefing starters on the board: 'Last month, … was opened/repaired' · 'Recently, … has been introduced' · 'It is expected that … will be completed…'

• If a learner drops 'be' ('The rules changed yesterday' when passive is intended), have them tap two fingers on the desk — one for 'was/were' and one for the past participle.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to use 'is believed to have + participle' for past reported events and a 'Founded / Built in…' participle opener in their Real Talk briefing.

• Ask stronger pairs to compare when the conversational 'get' passive ('He got promoted') fits and when the standard 'be' passive ('He was promoted') is better.

• Challenge early finishers to include a modal passive ('should be prioritised', 'can be accessed') in their closing recommendation.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'The house was builted in 1990.' → 'The house was built in 1990.' — Fix: review common irregular participles (built, written, chosen, spoken, stolen).

• 'My laptop was broken by me.' → 'I broke my laptop.' — Fix: keep your own actions active.

• 'A new policy has introduced.' → 'A new policy has been introduced.' — Fix: present perfect passive always needs 'been' before the participle.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two news updates per partner in the Part 5 Newsroom.

• Do the four-tense classroom object drill in Part 6 in class and assign the participle-opener sentences as homework.

• Run a 60-second Real Talk briefing per partner and finish with the Part 8 oral recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one past passive and one present perfect passive about their city.

• Remind learners that passive voice connects directly to Lesson 10 (Causatives) and appears in Review Test 3 and the Final Assessment.

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 9 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Praise reporters who maintained an objective news tone and shifted cleanly to active voice for their final comment. Then put two anonymous passive tense slips on the board for a 60-second class repair.

LESSON 10 · CAUSATIVE STRUCTURES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 5 — Describe and Explain | Speaking goal: talk about services, arrangements, influence and responsibility naturally

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Use 'have/get + object + past participle' accurately to describe professional services arranged by the speaker as well as unexpected misfortunes.

• Distinguish the four interpersonal causative verbs in speech: 'make + person + base verb' (force), 'let + person + base verb' (allow), 'have + person + base verb' (assign), and 'get + person + to + verb' (persuade).

• Deliver a natural one-minute story about a busy week combining service causatives, a minor mishap, and interpersonal causative verbs.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners place the object before the past participle in 'have/get something done' ('I had my laptop repaired', never 'I had repaired my laptop' or 'get my laptop to repair')

✓ learners use 'to' after 'get + person' ('got my brother to help') and bare infinitives after 'make', 'let', and 'have'

✓ in the passive, learners restore 'to' after 'made' ('We were made to wait')

Before class begins:

• Write the two core causative patterns on the board: (1) SERVICE / MISHAP: have / get + OBJECT + PAST PARTICIPLE ('have my suit cleaned'); (2) PEOPLE: make / let / have + PERSON + BASE VERB vs get + PERSON + TO + VERB.

• Write the contrast pair 'I painted my flat' (my own hands) vs 'I had my flat painted' (I hired a painter) on the board for Part 1.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two sentence pairs in Part 1 aloud ('I cut my hair' vs 'I had my hair cut'; 'My older brother fixed my laptop' vs 'I got my older brother to fix my laptop') and explain who held the scissors and how the brother was convinced.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to answer the two personal hook questions (tasks they do themselves vs services they pay someone else to do, and what teachers or parents made or let them do at school).

• Point out how English packs 'I arranged for a professional to do this for me' into a four-word pattern.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 ('have/get something done'): drill the word order 'have/get + object + past participle' across tenses and contrast arranged services ('I had my watch repaired') with unexpected mishaps ('He had his wallet stolen').

• Teach Rule 2 ('make, let, have, and get + person'): highlight the memory hook — 'make, let, and have take the bare verb; only get takes to' — and note that passive 'be made to + verb' brings 'to' back.

• Teach Rule 3 (Everyday service chunks): chorally practise 'get my hair cut', 'have the brakes checked', 'get a document translated', and 'have my photo taken'.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'I will get my car to repair tomorrow' — how do we fix this causative? ('I will get my car repaired tomorrow' — object + past participle.)

• 'The teacher made us to rewrite the essay' vs 'We were made to rewrite the essay' — why is the first wrong and the second right? (Active 'make' takes a bare verb; passive 'be made' takes 'to'.)

• Which of the four verbs ('make', 'let', 'have', 'get') requires 'to' before the action in active sentences? ('get' — 'got him to help'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, Doing It Yourself vs Arranging a Service vs Suffering a Mishap; second, the four interpersonal verbs ('made me stay' / 'let me leave' / 'had the assistant book' / 'got my friend to help').

• Run a quick oral check: say 'I paid a mechanic to service my car', and have the class answer with 'I had/got my car serviced.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking A1 ('repaired'), A3 ('lose' after 'made'), and A6 ('to eat' after 'get').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners transform B1–B2, repair B3 and B4 aloud, and share their true sentences for B5 and B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class and chorally repair B3 ('get my car repaired') and B4 ('made me wait').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. altered · 2. cut · 3. lose · 4. use · 5. tested · 6. to turn

Practice B: 1. I had my car serviced last week. · 2. After a long discussion, I got my friend to drive us to the airport. · 3. I will get my laptop repaired tomorrow. · 4. The security guard made us wait outside in the rain. · 5. answers vary (e.g. 'I had my watch battery replaced on Monday.') · 6. Could I have my phone screen replaced today? / How much would it cost to get my phone screen replaced?

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'repaired' — past participle after 'had my watch…'.

• A3 'lose' — bare infinitive after active 'made me…'.

• A6 'to eat' — 'get + person + to + verb' for persuasion.

• B1 'I had my car serviced last week' (or 'got my car serviced').

• B3 repairs 'to repair' to 'repaired'; B4 repairs 'to wait' to 'wait'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how two partners plan an event or office move using 'have the invitations printed', 'get the projector checked', 'have the technician test…', and 'got my cousin to lend…'.

• Give pairs four minutes to choose one of the two scenarios in Part 5 (preparing for a big family wedding or setting up a new office/study centre) and agree on their plan using at least three 'have/get something done' structures and two 'make/let/have/get + person' structures.

• Have two pairs report their plan to the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: For the conference on Saturday, we still need to have the programme booklets printed and get the sound system tested. B: I can have the technician check the microphones tomorrow morning, and I've already got Tariq to design the welcome banner. A: Great — will the venue manager let us set up the tables on Friday evening? B: Yes, she let us have the keys after five, as long as we don't make the security staff stay past nine.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): each learner says four true sentences about their own life (two services they have done regularly, one thing they got a friend to help with, and one rule a teacher or manager made them follow).

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise workplace delegation ('I'll have the team send you the figures'), expressive 'had us all laughing', and 'get around to + verb-ing' ('I finally got around to having my eyes tested').

• Ask pairs to compare the tone of 'I'll have my assistant call you' with 'I'll ask my assistant to call you'.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to jot down three keywords for their one-minute 'busy week' story: (1) a service they arranged, (2) an unexpected problem or mishap, and (3) how someone made, let, or got them to handle it.

• Partners take turns speaking for one full minute while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist items.

• Uncover the Model response, notice how it links 'I had to get my passport photo taken and have my degree certificates translated', 'I had my umbrella blown inside out', 'made me fill in…', and 'got my brother to pick me up', and have learners refine one line of their story.

Student Book model response:

Last Thursday started badly from the moment I woke up. I had had my car serviced the evening before, yet when I turned the key it still wouldn't start, so I got my neighbour to check the battery before he left for work. Then, on the bus into town, I almost had my bag taken in the crowd. When I arrived twenty minutes late, my manager made me reschedule my morning client call, but she kindly let me use her quiet office to prepare for the afternoon presentation. By five o'clock, I had the garage tow the car in and replace the starter motor — and the whole chaotic day had us laughing over dinner.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four Partner listening checklist targets: 'have/get + object + past participle' for services, a second causative for a repair or mishap, 'make/let/have + bare verb', and 'get + person + to + verb'.

• Accept any real or realistic busy-week narrative.

• Collect two anonymous word-order or 'to'-insertion slips for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (three things to have/get done this month and contrasting 'made me do' with 'let me do').

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 10 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Leave the two board formulas visible during Pair Speaking and Real Talk so developing speakers can check whether they are talking about an OBJECT (past participle) or a PERSON (base verb / to + verb).

• Provide simple starters: 'First, I had my… fixed/checked' · 'My manager made/let me…' · 'Luckily, I got my friend to…'

• If a learner says 'I had repaired my car', write 'I had [MY CAR] [REPAIRED]' in two boxes on the board and have them point to the object box first.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to weave in 'got around to having… done' and 'had us all laughing / worried' during their Real Talk story.

• Challenge stronger pairs to include one passive 'was made to…' or ' wasn't allowed to…' contrast in their conversation.

• Ask early finishers to discuss how causative structures make business negotiations sound concise and professional.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'I'll get my laptop to fix.' → 'I'll get my laptop fixed.' — Fix: after 'have/get + object', always use the past participle.

• 'He made me to apologise.' → 'He made me apologise.' — Fix: no 'to' after active 'make', 'let', or 'have'.

• 'I had cut my hair yesterday.' → 'I had my hair cut yesterday.' — Fix: put the object ('my hair') between 'had' and the past participle.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run one planning scenario in Part 5 for 3 minutes.

• Do the four personal causative sentences in Part 6 in class and assign the 'got around to…' extension as homework.

• Run one 60-second Real Talk story per partner and finish with the Part 8 recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one 'have/get something done' sentence and one 'get someone to do' sentence before leaving.

• Remind learners that causatives are tested in Review Test 3 (A2, C3) and the Final Assessment (A8, B7).

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 10 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Praise speakers who combined service causatives with 'got someone to…' naturally in their busy-week story. Then put two anonymous 'made me to…' or 'get it to repair' slips on the board for a quick class repair.

LESSON 11 · GERUNDS AND INFINITIVES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 6 — Speak with Greater Precision | Speaking goal: choose the right verb pattern for your meaning

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Choose accurately between the gerund ('verb-ing') and the to-infinitive ('to + base verb') after common English verbs and expressions.

• Control meaning-changing verbs ('remember', 'forget', 'stop', 'try') where switching between '-ing' and 'to + verb' changes the real-world event.

• Use 'verb-ing' consistently after prepositions, including expressions where 'to' is a preposition ('look forward to + verb-ing', 'be used to + verb-ing').

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners use '-ing' after 'enjoy', 'avoid', 'mind', 'suggest', and 'keep', and 'to + verb' after 'decide', 'hope', 'plan', 'promise', and 'refuse'

✓ learners use '-ing' after 'look forward to' and 'be/get used to' without slipping into the base verb

✓ in Pair Speaking and Real Talk, speakers accurately use at least one meaning-changing verb ('stop', 'remember', or 'try')

Before class begins:

• Write three clear columns on the board: (1) VERB + -ING ('enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest, finish, keep') · (2) VERB + TO + BASE VERB ('decide, plan, hope, promise, offer, refuse') · (3) PREPOSITION + -ING ('interested in, good at, instead of, look forward to, be used to').

• Write the contrast pair 'He stopped smoking' vs 'He stopped to smoke' on the board for Part 1.

Lesson step
