Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two sentence pairs in Part 1 aloud ('He stopped smoking' vs 'He stopped to smoke'; 'I remembered locking the door' vs 'I remembered to lock the door') and decide who quit a habit and when the memory happened.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to complete the four personal stems in Part 1 aloud ('After a long week, I really enjoy…', 'This year, I've decided…', 'When I have a deadline, I try to avoid…', and 'Next month, I'm really looking forward to…').

• Show learners that learning verb patterns as two-word spoken chunks ('enjoy reading', 'decide to apply', 'look forward to meeting') makes the choice automatic.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Verbs followed by '-ing'): have the class read the chunk list aloud and spotlight two high-value traps — 'Would you mind opening…?' and 'She suggested taking…' (never 'suggested me to take').

• Teach Rule 2 (Verbs followed by 'to + base verb'): point out how future-oriented verbs ('decide', 'plan', 'hope', 'promise', 'expect') and 'verb + person + to + verb' ('advise/remind/encourage someone to…') point forward toward a goal.

• Teach Rule 3 (Verbs whose meaning changes): explain the timeline principle — '-ing' looks back at an existing or earlier action ('remember locking', 'stopped talking'), whereas 'to + verb' looks forward to a new action or purpose ('remember to lock', 'stopped to buy').

• Teach Rule 4 (Prepositions + '-ing'): drill 'look forward to hearing', 'be used to waking up', and 'instead of waiting' chorally.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'I look forward to meet you on Monday' — why do we need 'meeting' after 'to' here? (Because 'to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition — test it with a noun: 'I look forward to the meeting'.)

• 'She suggested me to take the train' — how do we repair this sentence? ('She suggested taking the train' or 'She suggested that I take the train'.)

• 'I stopped buying coffee on the way to work' vs 'I stopped to buy coffee on the way to work' — who saved money? (The first speaker — 'stopped buying' means quit the habit.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the meaning-changing table in Part 3 ('stopped checking' vs 'stopped to check'; 'remembered calling' vs 'remembered to call'; 'tried restarting' vs 'tried to fix') and the 'need + -ing' ('needs charging') vs 'need + to' note.

• Ask pairs to test each other: Partner A reads one sentence from the table, and Partner B explains which action happened first.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking A2 ('criticising'), A4 ('hearing' after 'look forward to'), and the A5/A6 'stopped' vs 'tried' pair.

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners repair B1–B3 aloud, produce both 'need' forms for B4, explain B5 ('posting' = memory of an earlier action), and say their 'Instead of + -ing' sentence for B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class and re-drill B2 ('look forward to meeting') and B3 ('suggested leaving') chorally.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. helping · 2. criticising · 3. to accept · 4. hearing · 5. smoking · 6. to open

Practice B: 1. I really enjoy reading historical biographies in the evening. · 2. We look forward to meeting your team on Monday. · 3. My colleague suggested leaving early before the snow started. / …suggested that we leave early… · 4. The classroom needs cleaning before tomorrow. / The classroom needs to be cleaned before tomorrow. · 5. posting (because I posted it first and I recall the memory of doing it now) · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Instead of cramming the night before an exam, I review my notes for fifteen minutes every evening.')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'helping' — 'Would you mind + verb-ing'.

• A4 'hearing' — 'look forward to + verb-ing'.

• A5 'smoking' (quit the habit) vs A6 'to open' (made a difficult attempt).

• B3 accepts 'My colleague suggested leaving early…' or 'My colleague suggested that we leave early…'.

• B4 'The classroom needs cleaning / The classroom needs to be cleaned before tomorrow.'

• B5 'posting' — the speaker has the receipt in their pocket, so they are looking back at a memory of an earlier action.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how the two partners use 'avoid checking', 'decided to leave', 'used to leaving', 'enjoy reading', and 'looking forward to visiting'.

• Run the four-minute Pair Speaking interview using the four prompts in Part 5, requiring at least one follow-up question after every answer.

• Have two learners report one habit their partner enjoys or avoids and one goal their partner plans to achieve.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: What is one distraction you always try to avoid when you're working? B: I avoid checking my phone in the morning — in fact, I've decided to leave it in another room until noon. A: Was it hard to get used to doing that? B: At first it was, but now I really enjoy having two quiet hours, and I'm looking forward to finishing my project early this week.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs practise the ten spoken chunks aloud and build true sentence pairs with 'stop + -ing / stop + to' and 'try + -ing / try + to'.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): introduce gerund subjects ('Speaking a second language in public takes courage'), evaluative frames ('It's worth + -ing', 'There's no point in + -ing', 'have difficulty + -ing'), and 'used to do' (past habit) vs 'be/get used to doing' (accustomed to).

• Have each learner build one 'used to do' + 'am used to doing' pair about a change in their life.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to jot down keywords for their one-minute talk on habits and goals: two '-ing' habits/activities, two 'to + verb' plans, one preposition + '-ing' phrase, and one meaning-changing verb.

• Partners take turns speaking for one full minute while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it weaves 'enjoy starting', 'avoid looking', 'tried studying', 'stopped studying… to practise', 'decided to take', and 'looking forward to joining', and have learners polish one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

Learning English as an adult has taught me to be much more patient with myself. When I first started, I tried translating every single word in my head before speaking, which only made me hesitate. Eventually I stopped doing that and practised listening for whole phrases instead. Nowadays I really enjoy reading short articles aloud in the morning, and I keep a small notebook for expressions worth remembering. I used to avoid speaking in front of larger groups, but this term I've decided to join our department's weekly discussion circle, and I look forward to testing my voice there.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four Partner listening checklist items: accurate '-ing' verbs, accurate 'to + verb' verbs, one preposition + '-ing' structure ('look forward to / used to / instead of + -ing'), and one meaning-changing verb.

• Praise natural chunk fluency rather than counting isolated grammar terms.

• Collect two anonymous slips (especially 'suggest someone to do' or 'look forward to + base verb') for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (contrasting 'stop' and 'remember' with '-ing' vs 'to', and naming five '-ing' verbs and five 'to' verbs from memory).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 11 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the three-column board chart visible during Parts 5 and 7 so developing speakers can glance at the verb chunks while speaking.

• Drill the five most useful two-word chunks chorally before Pair Speaking: 'enjoy doing · avoid doing · suggest doing · decide to do · look forward to doing'.

• If a learner hesitates on 'remember/stop + -ing vs to', ask: 'Did the action happen first (-ing), or was it the next goal (to)?'

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to open their Real Talk turn with a gerund subject ('Building a new habit takes…') and include 'It's worth + -ing' or 'have difficulty + -ing'.

• Challenge stronger pairs to use both 'used to + base verb' (past state/habit) and 'be/get used to + verb-ing' (becoming accustomed) in the same answer during Part 5.

• Ask early finishers to explain the difference between 'I regret telling him' (looking back at a past action) and 'We regret to inform you…' (formal announcement of bad news).

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'I really enjoy to read in the evening.' → 'I really enjoy reading in the evening.' — Fix: drill 'enjoy + -ing' as an inseparable chunk.

• 'We look forward to hear from you.' → 'We look forward to hearing from you.' — Fix: 'to' is a preposition here, so it takes '-ing'.

• 'He suggested me to apply.' → 'He suggested applying / that I apply.' — Fix: 'suggest' never takes 'person + to + verb' (contrast with 'He advised me to apply').

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two interview questions per partner in Part 5.

• Do the chunk and meaning-pair drill in Part 6 in class and assign the 'used to do / be used to doing' sentences as homework.

• Run a 60-second Real Talk turn per partner and close with the Part 8 oral recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner finishes 'This weekend I'm looking forward to…' and 'Next month I plan to…' aloud before leaving.

• Remind learners that gerunds and infinitives are tested in Review Test 3 (A4, C4) and the Final Assessment (A7, A11, C8).

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 11 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Quote one strong meaning-changing sentence ('I stopped scrolling and started reading…') you heard during Part 7, then put two anonymous preposition/verb-pattern slips on the board for a quick class repair.

LESSON 12 · RELATIVE CLAUSES AND CONCISE DESCRIPTIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 6 — Speak with Greater Precision | Speaking goal: describe people, places and ideas precisely in one sentence

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Use defining relative clauses ('who', 'which', 'that', 'whose', 'where', 'when') to identify people, things, and places precisely without repeating pronouns.

• Use non-defining relative clauses (with commas/spoken pauses and 'who/which/whose/where', never 'that') to add extra background information or comment on a whole situation.

• Compress relative clauses naturally by dropping object pronouns or omitting 'who/which/that + be' before '-ing' phrases, past participles, and adjective phrases.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners never use 'what' as a relative pronoun after a noun ('the book that I read', not 'the book what I read') and never use 'that' after a comma

✓ learners drop redundant object pronouns inside relative clauses ('the friend I told you about', not 'the friend who I told you about her')

✓ in the Real Talk Challenge, speakers combine a defining clause, a non-defining clause, a 'whose' or 'where' clause, and a concise reduced phrase

Before class begins:

• Write the two clause types on the board: (1) DEFINING (no commas — identifies WHICH ONE; 'who / which / that', object pronoun can drop); (2) NON-DEFINING (commas / brief pauses — adds EXTRA DETAIL; 'who / which / whose / where', NEVER 'that').

• Write the choppy four-sentence description and the smooth combined sentence from Part 1 on the board.

Lesson step

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two descriptions in Part 1 aloud (Speaker A's choppy four-sentence chain vs Speaker B's smooth one-sentence description) and notice how relative clauses weave separate facts into one clear portrait.

• Run the 90-second guessing game in Part 1: each learner describes one famous place in their country and one object in their bag using 'It's a place where…' and 'It's something that…' without naming it, while their partner guesses.

• Explain that relative clauses give speakers three powers: identifying, adding background detail, and compressing descriptions.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Defining relative clauses): walk through 'who/that' (people), 'which/that' (things), 'whose' (possession), and 'where' (place), and show when the relative pronoun can be dropped (when it is the OBJECT of the clause: 'the laptop [that] I bought').

• Teach Rule 2 (Non-defining relative clauses): contrast 'My brother who lives in Herat' with 'My brother, who lives in Herat,' and stress that 'that' is never used after a comma.

• Teach Rule 3 (Prepositions in relative clauses): compare formal 'the colleague with whom I worked' with natural spoken 'the colleague I worked with'.

• Teach Rule 4 (Reduced relative clauses): show how dropping 'who/which/that + be' produces crisp phrases ('the woman standing by the window', 'courses taught in English', 'students interested in the trip') — and why we cannot reduce an ordinary active verb like 'the man who called'.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'My mother, that lives in Kabul, is a doctor' — why is 'that' wrong here, and what replaces it? ('who' — never use 'that' in a non-defining clause after a comma.)

• 'The book what I read was fascinating' — why is 'what' wrong after 'the book'? ('what' means 'the thing that'; after a noun, use 'that', 'which', or nothing: 'The book I read…'.)

• Can we reduce 'the woman who is waiting outside' to 'the woman waiting outside'? What about 'the woman who phoned yesterday'? (Yes to the first — 'who is' drops before '-ing'; no to the second — 'phoned' is a single past action.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, Defining vs Non-Defining ('how many brothers?' and 'all battery cars vs subset'); second, Full vs Reduced Relative Clauses.

• Have pairs read the defining vs non-defining brother sentences aloud, using a slight voice pause at the commas in the non-defining version so their partner can hear the difference.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking A2 ('which' after a comma), A3 ('whose'), and A5 ('built / which were built').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners combine B1, reduce B2, repair B3–B5, and deliver their two-clause description of an admired person for B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class, spotlighting the three classic repairs in B3 ('who' after a comma), B4 (no 'what' after a noun), and B5 (removing the redundant pronoun 'it').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. who · 2. which · 3. where · 4. whose · 5. which / that (or omit 'which/that were' to form the reduced clause 'The survey results published this morning…') · 6. that / which

Practice B: 1. The instructor who taught us academic speaking last term is outstanding. · 2. My uncle, who is an experienced airline pilot, has flown to over forty countries. / My uncle, who has flown to over forty countries, is an experienced airline pilot. · 3. My mother, who lives in Kandahar, is visiting us next Friday. · 4. The article (that / which) I read on the train was eye-opening. · 5. Students interested in the summer internship should apply online. · 6. answers vary

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A2 'which' — non-defining clause after a comma requires 'which' (never 'that').

• A5 accepts 'built' (reduced relative phrase) or 'which were built / that were built' (full clause).

• A6 'who / that' — subject of 'helped me', so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped.

• B3 repairs ', that' to ', who'; B4 repairs 'what' to '(that / which)'; B5 removes the redundant object pronoun 'it' ('The film (that) we watched last night was gripping').

• B6 is open — credit any description that accurately combines one defining and one non-defining clause.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how Speaker A layers a defining clause, a reduced phrase, and a non-defining clause in the guessing game.

• Run the four-minute Definition & Guessing Game in pairs: each partner secretly chooses one person, one place, and one object/profession and describes each in two sentences for their partner to guess — then compresses one sentence into a reduced relative phrase.

• Have two learners share their most concise clue with the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: I'm thinking of a place in our city that is always busy in the late afternoon. The street, which was renovated two years ago, is full of small bookshops selling second-hand textbooks. B: Is it the book market near the university? A: Spot on — it's the place where I bought all my exam guides last semester.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs build four true sentences using 'who', 'which/that' (dropped), 'whose', and 'where'.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise whole-clause commenting ', which…' ('She apologised immediately, which changed the whole mood'), 'What… is…' focus frames ('What I really appreciate is…'), and concise reduced noun phrases.

• Have each learner build one ', which…' comment sentence about something good that happened this week.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to choose a person who influenced them or a place that means a lot to them and jot down four keywords: (1) Defining role, (2) Non-defining background detail, (3) 'whose' or 'where' detail, and (4) Reduced relative phrase.

• Partners take turns speaking for one full minute while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it combines 'Dr Rahimi, who taught our first-year history seminar, is the professor who changed…', 'a teacher whose feedback was always honest', 'articles written by different historians', and ', which made every student feel capable', and have learners polish one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

The person who influenced my study habits most is my uncle, who taught secondary-school physics for over thirty years. He is the person whose advice I still hear whenever I sit down to tackle a difficult project: always start with the part that scares you most. The students taught by him at our local school respected him because he never lost his patience, which made even shy learners brave enough to ask questions. Anyone working alongside him quickly learns the same quiet lesson — steady preparation beats last-minute talent every time.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Evaluate the one-minute descriptions using the four Partner listening checklist items: defining clause, non-defining clause (with brief spoken pauses), 'whose' or 'where' clause, and a reduced relative phrase.

• Count the reduced clause in the Real Talk Challenge: credit any natural reduction where 'who/which/that + be' is omitted before an -ing form, past participle, or adjective phrase.

• Collect two anonymous pronoun or redundant-object slips ('the place where I went there') for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (one defining + one non-defining clause about the classroom, and a three-clause city description including a reduced phrase).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and remind them that Review Test 3 (Lessons 1–12) follows this lesson.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the Defining vs Non-Defining board chart visible during Parts 5 and 7 so developing speakers can check pronoun choices at a glance.

• Offer four clean description starters on the board: '…is someone who…' · '…, who/which…, …' · '…is a person whose…' · '…is the place where…'

• If a learner repeats the object pronoun ('the friend who I met him'), write the sentence on the board and show how 'who' already replaces 'him'.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to include one whole-clause ', which…' comment and one 'What… is…' focus frame during Part 7.

• Challenge stronger pairs to compress two clauses into a single sentence using both a non-defining clause and a reduced participle phrase.

• Ask early finishers to compare formal 'the professor with whom I spoke' and conversational 'the professor I spoke with' for different speaking contexts.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'The book what I read was great.' → 'The book (that) I read was great.' — Fix: never use 'what' after a noun.

• 'My uncle, that is an engineer, helped me.' → 'My uncle, who is an engineer, helped me.' — Fix: after a comma, use 'who' or 'which', never 'that'.

• 'That's the café where we met there.' → 'That's the café where we met.' — Fix: 'where' already means 'there', so drop 'there'.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two guessing items per partner in Part 5.

• Do the four-pronoun drill in Part 6 in class and assign the ', which…' and 'What… is…' sentences as written homework.

• Run one 60-second Real Talk description per partner and finish with the Part 8 recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner describes a classmate or place in the city using one defining clause and one non-defining clause.

• Remind learners that Review Test 3 (covering Lessons 1–12) follows this lesson; point them to Formula Book Cards 1–12 in Appendix 1.

• Note that reduced relative phrases connect directly to Lesson 14 (Participles).

• Feedback focus: Praise descriptions that painted a clear picture and used natural voice pauses for non-defining details. Then put two anonymous relative-clause slips on the board and let pairs repair them together.

LESSON 13 · REPORTED SPEECH AND REPORTING VERBS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: report conversations and summarise information accurately and naturally

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Report statements, questions, and requests/commands accurately using tense backshift, pronoun shifts, and statement word order.

• Use expressive reporting verbs ('admit', 'promise', 'warn', 'remind', 'suggest', 'deny') with their natural verb patterns to capture the original speaker's intention.

• Retell a memorable real-life conversation in 90 seconds using at least four different reporting verbs, one reported question, and one reported request or warning.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners distinguish 'say (that)…' from 'tell + person (that)…' without saying 'He said me…'

✓ reported questions use embedded statement word order ('She asked me where I lived', never 'where did I live')

✓ reporting verbs in Practice B and speaking tasks match their required grammatical pattern ('suggested going', 'warned me not to go', 'promised to help')

Before class begins:

• Write the Backshift Ladder on the board: Present ('am/is/do') → Past ('was/did') · Past / Present Perfect → Past Perfect ('had done') · 'will' → 'would' · 'can' → 'could'.

• Write the three reporting-verb pattern groups on the board: (1) VERB + TO ('promise, offer, agree, refuse') · (2) VERB + PERSON + (NOT) TO ('tell, ask, advise, warn, remind') · (3) VERB + -ING ('admit, deny, suggest').

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two versions of the meeting in Part 1 aloud (Speaker A's robotic 'he said… she said…' quotes vs Speaker B's natural summary with 'pointed out', 'suggested', 'asked whether', and 'promised') and discuss why Speaker B sounds far more professional.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to report three real things people said to them this week — one statement, one question, and one piece of advice or request.

• Show learners that reporting speech is not about repeating every word verbatim — it is about summarising meaning, tone, and perspective.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Backshift in reported statements): walk down the board ladder and note when a speaker can keep the present tense (when reporting a fact that is still true right now: 'She said she lives in Kabul').

• Teach Rule 2 (Reporting questions, requests, and commands): connect reported questions directly to Lesson 3's indirect questions — drop 'do/does/did' and use 'if/whether' or a question word + Subject + Verb ('asked me where I worked') — and drill 'told/asked/warned + person + (not) to'.

• Teach Rule 3 (Reporting verbs beyond 'say' and 'tell') and Rule 4 (Shifting time and place words: 'tomorrow → the next day', 'yesterday → the day before', 'here → there').

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'He said me that he was busy' — how do we fix this in two different ways? ('He told me that he was busy' or 'He said that he was busy'.)

• 'She asked me where did I buy my laptop' — how do we fix the word order? ('She asked me where I had bought / bought my laptop' — statement order, no 'did'.)

• 'My friend suggested me to take the early bus' — why is 'me to take' wrong after 'suggest', and what is the fix? ('suggested taking the early bus' or 'suggested that I take…'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two tables in Part 3: first, the four-verb contrast between 'say', 'tell', 'ask', and 'suggest'; second, Direct Speech vs Natural Reported Speech across statements, questions, warnings, and suggestions.

• Run a 30-second choral repair on the two classic traps: 'He said me…' → 'He told me…' and 'She suggested me to wait' → 'She suggested waiting / that I wait.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking A2 ('if/whether I liked'), A3 ('where the station was'), A4 ('not to'), and A6 ('taking').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners report B1–B2, repair B3 and B4 aloud, and rewrite B5 ('denied breaking') and B6 ('promised to help').

• Confirm the key whole-class and have pairs read B1 and B2 aloud with shifted time phrases.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. was working · 2. had already submitted · 3. had parked (or: parked) · 4. not to · 5. to help · 6. taking

Practice B: 1. He said (that) he never drank coffee after six in the evening. / He said (that) he never drinks coffee after six in the evening. · 2. They asked when the scholarship results would be announced. · 3. He told me that the train had been cancelled. / He said that the train had been cancelled. · 4. My colleague suggested applying for the fellowship. / My colleague suggested that I apply for the fellowship. · 5. He denied sharing the password with anyone. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'My teacher advised me to read aloud every morning, and my mother reminded me not to skip breakfast before an exam.')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'was working' — backshift from present continuous 'am working'.

• A3 'was' — statement word order after 'asked me where the station…'.

• A4 'not to' — negative warning/command ('warned the children not to touch').

• A6 'taking' — 'suggest + verb-ing'.

• B5 'He denied breaking the window' (or 'denied having broken'); B6 'She promised to help me with the report.'

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how Speaker A weaves 'told me', 'admitted', 'warned her not to', 'asked me if', 'suggested', and 'promised' into a natural conversation summary.

• Run the four-minute Relay & Retell activity in pairs: each partner chooses two situations from Part 5 (a job interview, a doctor/mentor visit, a trip plan, or a resolved misunderstanding) and reports what was said using at least four different reporting verbs, one reported question, and one reported request/warning.

• Ask two listeners to summarise their partner's best reported exchange for the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: I spoke to my cousin last night before her job interview. She told me she was feeling nervous and admitted she hadn't practised her answers out loud yet. B: What did you advise her to do? A: I suggested doing a ten-minute mock interview together on the phone, warned her not to speak too fast, and promised to call her again this evening.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs practise the backshift ladder and build four true sentences from their week using 'promised to', 'reminded me to', 'admitted -ing', and 'suggested -ing'.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): introduce narrative frames ('kept insisting that…', 'went on to explain that…'), academic/present reporting ('The report points out that…'), and stance verbs ('claimed to have…' vs 'established that…').

• Ask pairs to discuss how choosing 'claimed' vs 'explained' changes the listener's trust in the original speaker.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to choose a real conversation that mattered to them and jot down four keywords (who spoke, what was stated, what was asked, and what was advised or promised).

• Partners take turns speaking for 90 seconds while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it moves from 'asked me whether I had ever spoken…' to 'admitted that I felt…' to 'advised me not to memorise…' and 'suggested writing…', and have learners refine one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

Last Saturday my younger sister called to tell me that she had been offered a position at a graphic design studio. She admitted that she felt nervous about the tight deadlines, but she promised to give it her best effort for the first six months. Our father warned her not to sign the contract without checking the evening hours first, and she agreed to ask the director for a written schedule. She also asked me whether I thought she should negotiate the starting salary; I suggested showing them her portfolio from university before naming a figure. In the end, they offered her a better rate than she had expected.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Listen for the four Partner listening checklist targets: four varied reporting verbs, one reported question with statement word order, one reported request/warning ('told/asked/warned + person + (not) to'), and natural tense/time shifts.

• Credit present tense in reported clauses when the speaker is clearly stating a permanent or still-true fact.

• Collect two anonymous slips ('said me', 'asked where was…', or 'suggested me to…') for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (reporting three sentences from today's class and reporting one question, one warning, and one suggestion).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 13 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep both the Backshift Ladder and the three Reporting-Verb Pattern groups visible on the board during Parts 5 and 7.

• Provide four ready-to-use reporting starters: 'She asked me whether…' · 'I admitted that…' · 'He advised me (not) to…' · 'She suggested + verb-ing…'

• If a learner keeps inverting reported questions, point to the 'Indirect Questions' rule from Lesson 3: 'asked where + SUBJECT + VERB'.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to include 'went on to explain that…', 'kept insisting that…', or 'claimed to have + participle' during their 90-second story.

• Challenge stronger pairs to summarise a news article or workplace report using present-tense reporting verbs ('points out', 'argues', 'demonstrates').

• Ask early finishers to compare 'She reminded me to lock the door' (before the action) with 'She reminded me that I had locked the door' (confirming a fact).

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'He said me that the meeting was cancelled.' → 'He told me that… / He said that…' — Fix: 'tell' takes a person; 'say' does not.

• 'She asked me what time does the bank open.' → 'She asked me what time the bank opened.' — Fix: use statement order and backshift the verb.

• 'They suggested us to wait.' → 'They suggested waiting / that we wait.' — Fix: 'suggest' never takes 'person + to + verb'.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; have each partner report one situation in depth during Part 5.

• Do the four reporting-verb chunks in Part 6 in class and assign the academic/narrative reporting frames as homework.

• Run a 60-second Real Talk story per partner and close with the Part 8 oral recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner reports one question and one piece of advice they heard today.

• Remind learners that reported speech appears in the Final Assessment (items B1, B2, and C7).

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 13 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Praise speakers who used expressive verbs ('admitted', 'warned', 'suggested', 'promised') instead of repeating 'said'. Then put two anonymous reported-question or verb-pattern slips on the board for a quick whole-class repair.

LESSON 14 · PARTICIPLES AND ADVANCED SENTENCE PATTERNS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: combine ideas concisely without losing clarity

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Distinguish '-ing' adjectives (the cause of a feeling) from '-ed' adjectives (the person who experiences the feeling) in everyday and professional descriptions.

• Use present, past, and perfect participle clauses ('Walking…', 'Built in…', 'Having finished…') to combine ideas concisely while keeping the subject matched to the main clause.

• Deliver a formal 90-second briefing or recommendation using 'Given / Considering + noun', a 'Having + past participle' clause, and a 'With + noun + -ing' structure.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ zero confusion between '-ing' and '-ed' adjectives ('interested in', 'exhausting day')

✓ every opening participle clause shares the exact same subject as the main clause (no dangling participles like 'Opening the window, the room was cold')

✓ in the Real Talk briefing, speakers use at least two participle clauses and one 'Given / Considering' or 'With + noun + -ing' frame naturally

Before class begins:

• Write the Adjective Rule and the Subject-Match Rule on the board: (1) -ING = CAUSES THE FEELING ('a fascinating lecture') vs -ED = FEELS IT ('a fascinated audience'); (2) PARTICIPLE SUBJECT MUST MATCH MAIN SUBJECT ('[Having finished the report], [she] sent it').

• Write the three formal briefing frames on the board: 'Given / Considering + noun, …' · 'Having + past participle, …' · 'With + noun + verb-ing, …'.

Lesson step

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two sentence pairs in Part 1 aloud ('I am very interesting in history' vs 'I am very interested in history'; the three-sentence report vs 'Having reviewed the budget, the director approved the plan') and explain why the right-hand sentences sound so much more natural and professional.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to describe one exhausting or exciting experience from this month using both an '-ing' and an '-ed' adjective, and to combine 'She finished her presentation. She answered three questions from the audience.' into a single smooth sentence.

• Introduce participles as the tool that gives spoken briefings and presentations concision and authority.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 ('-ing' vs '-ed' adjectives): chorally drill four high-frequency pairs ('interesting/interested', 'tiring/tired', 'confusing/confused', 'encouraging/encouraged').

• Teach Rule 2 (Participle clauses — 'Doing', 'Done', and 'Having done') and Rule 4 (Compressing two clauses without a dangling subject): draw an arrow on the board from 'Having reviewed the figures' to 'we' and contrast it with the broken 'Opening the window, the room felt cold.'

• Teach Rule 3 (Prepositional and absolute frames): show how 'Given the tight deadline, …', 'Considering the cost, …', and 'With energy prices rising, …' allow a speaker to set the context cleanly at the start of a recommendation.

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'I am very interesting in this topic' — why does that make listeners smile, and what is the fix? ('I am very interested in this topic' — people feel '-ed'; things cause the feeling with '-ing'.)

• 'Opening the front door, the dog ran out' — who opened the front door according to the grammar? (The dog! Fix: 'Opening the front door, I saw the dog run out' or 'When I opened the front door…'.)

• Why doesn't 'Given the high cost, the plan was delayed' count as a dangling participle? (Because 'Given' and 'Considering' are fixed framing prepositions meaning 'taking into account'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, '-ing' (Cause) vs '-ed' (Feeling); second, Full Clauses vs Participle Compression (including the Dangling vs Matched Subject row).

• Have pairs repair 'Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful' aloud in two ways ('Walking down the street, I admired the trees' or 'As I was walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful').

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking A1/A2 ('boring / bored'), A3 ('Having finished'), A4 ('Built'), and A5 ('With').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners compress B1–B2, repair the dangling participle in B3 and the adjective error in B5, and build their 'Given…' sentence for B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class and chorally practise the repaired B3 ('Opening the window, I felt the cold air').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. boring · 2. amazed · 3. Having finished · 4. Warned / Having been warned · 5. With · 6. Walking

Practice B: 1. Having practised her talk five times, she spoke without hesitation. · 2. The technician standing by the generator switched off the power. · 3. Opening the window, I felt the fresh morning breeze cool the room. / When I opened the window, the fresh morning breeze cooled the room. · 4. Given the tight deadline, the team's report is very thorough. · 5. I have always been very interested in architectural history. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Having had a cup of green tea, I sat down to read Lesson 14.')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'boring' (the lecture causes the feeling); A2 'bored' (the students feel it).

• A3 'Having finished' — earlier action completed before she went out.

• A4 'Built' — past participle (passive meaning: 'Because it was built in 1920…').

• B1 'Having studied hard, he passed the exam.'

• B3 'Opening the window, I felt the cold air' (matches the subject 'I' to 'Opening').

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn Formal Briefing model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how Speaker A combines 'Given the tight deadline', 'Having worked late', 'encouraging', 'impressed', and 'With demand growing'.

• Run the four-minute Formal Briefing in pairs: each partner delivers a 60-second briefing on one of the three workplace/campus scenarios in Part 5 while the listener prepares a one-sentence executive summary and one follow-up question.

• Invite two pairs to share their briefing and one-sentence summary with the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: Given the short deadline, our team delivered the new training schedule on time. Having tested the materials with a small group first, we felt confident about the launch. B: How did the participants react? A: The feedback was very encouraging, and the new instructors were genuinely excited. With twenty more students joining next month, we recommend adding a second evening session.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): each learner says two true sentences with '-ing/-ed' pairs and two true sentences opening with 'Having + past participle' and 'Given + noun'.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): introduce negative participle openings ('Not wanting to wake the family, …', 'Never having spoken in front of a large crowd, …'), formal 'There being no further questions, …', and 'recommend + verb-ing'.

• Have each learner build one 'Not wanting to…' or 'Never having…' sentence about a real moment.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to choose one topic in Part 7 (recommending an improvement at work/school, evaluating a project, or explaining a major lesson) and jot down keywords for the three-part briefing plan.

• Partners take turns speaking for 90 seconds while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it uses 'Given the rapid growth…', 'Having surveyed over sixty learners…', 'overwhelmed… encouraging', and 'With class sizes increasing…', and have learners refine one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

Given the number of late arrivals during the winter months, I would recommend shifting our first morning seminar from eight o'clock to eight-thirty. Having reviewed the attendance logs from last January, our committee noticed that almost all delays occurred before eight-fifteen, when icy roads make the morning commute frustrating for drivers and passengers alike. Many tired students walk in ten minutes late, missing the opening explanation of the lecture. With classes starting just thirty minutes later, everyone could travel more safely and arrive focused. All things considered, a one-month winter trial costs nothing and would benefit the entire department.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Evaluate the 90-second briefings using the four Partner listening checklist criteria: 'Given / Considering' opener, 'Having + past participle' clause with matched subject, accurate '-ing/-ed' adjectives, and a 'With + noun + -ing' or passive participle phrase.

• Remind speakers that one or two well-placed participle clauses per briefing sound crisp and authoritative — don't try to cram one into every sentence.

• Repair any dangling participle on the board immediately after the round.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (one 'Having…' sentence + one 'Given…' sentence, and repairing 'Walking into the room, the lights were off').

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 14 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the Subject-Match arrow and the three Briefing Frames visible on the board during Parts 5 and 7.

• Teach developing speakers a simple self-check before saying a 'Having…' sentence: 'Ask Who? right after the comma — and make that person the very next word.'

• If a learner mixes up '-ing' and '-ed', use the quick cue: 'Thing = -ing · Person's feeling = -ed.'

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to include a negative participle clause ('Not wanting to delay the project, …' or 'Never having used the software before, …') in their briefing.

• Challenge stronger pairs to close their recommendation with 'We therefore recommend + verb-ing…' or 'We recommend that the committee + base verb…'.

• Ask early finishers to compare when a reduced relative phrase (Lesson 12) and a fronted participle clause (Lesson 14) work best in formal presentations.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'Walking down the street, a car almost hit me.' → 'Walking down the street, I was almost hit by a car / As I was walking…' — Fix: match the subject right after the comma.

• 'The instructions were very confused.' → 'The instructions were very confusing.' — Fix: instructions cause confusion (-ing); people feel confused (-ed).

• 'Having finish the work, he left.' → 'Having finished the work, he left.' — Fix: 'Having' is always followed by the past participle.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run one 60-second briefing per partner in Part 5.

• Do the '-ing/-ed' and 'Having/Given' sentences in Part 6 in class and assign the negative participle sentences as homework.

• Run a 60-second Real Talk briefing per partner and finish with the Part 8 oral recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one 'Having + participle' sentence and one 'Given + noun' sentence before leaving.

• Remind learners that participle clauses are tested in the Final Assessment (items A10 and B10).

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 14 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Praise briefings that combined 'Given…' and 'Having…' with a matched subject right after the comma. Then draw one anonymous dangling participle on the board and let pairs fix the subject together.

LESSON 15 · HEDGING, EMPHASIS, AND NATURAL INVERSION — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: control certainty, emphasis and formality like an educated speaker

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Use measured hedging language ('may well', 'tends to', 'is likely to', ' the evidence suggests', 'it could be argued that') so claims match the strength of the evidence.

• Spotlight key information using 'It-clefts' ('It was X that…'), 'What-clefts' ('What matters most is…'), and auxiliary 'do/does/did' emphasis.

• Use negative and limiting inversion ('Never have I…', 'Rarely do we…', 'Not only did…, but…', 'Only after… did…') sparingly and accurately for high-impact moments.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners invert the auxiliary before the subject after negative openers ('Never have I seen…', 'Not only did she…')

✓ learners hedge predictions and generalisations appropriately without stacking three hedges in one clause

✓ in the two-minute Real Talk speech, speakers combine measured hedging, one cleft sentence, and one negative inversion naturally

Before class begins:

• Write the three tools on the board: (1) HEDGING (calibrate certainty: 'may well / tends to / the data suggest'); (2) CLEFT FOCUS ('It was X who/that…' · 'What we need is…'); (3) NEGATIVE INVERSION (Negative opener + Auxiliary + Subject + Verb: 'Rarely have we…' · 'Not only did they…').

• Write the two contrast pairs from Part 1 on the board (sweeping overstatement vs calibrated claim; flat statement vs cleft + inversion).

Lesson step

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

4

Practice the Pattern

Pair Speaking

Say It with Greater Precision

9

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two sentence pairs in Part 1 aloud ('Remote work destroys team culture' vs 'Remote work can weaken team culture if communication is poor…'; 'We need practical training…' vs 'What we need is practical training — rarely have I seen…') and discuss which speaker sounds more credible and persuasive.

• Give pairs 90 seconds to soften 'University exams are a waste of time' into a balanced claim and to spotlight the most important word in 'Clear feedback helps learners improve.'

• Establish the lesson's guiding principle: hedging protects your credibility, while clefts and inversion spotlight your most important point.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (Hedging — matching your certainty to your evidence): walk through the three levels (strong probability 'may well / is likely to', general tendency 'tends to / generally', and impersonal evidence 'The evidence suggests / It could be argued') and warn against over-hedging.

• Teach Rule 2 (Cleft sentences and 'do' emphasis): show how 'It was the practical workshop that…' and 'What makes the difference is…' place a verbal spotlight on the exact point the speaker wants the listener to remember.

• Teach Rule 3 (Negative and limiting inversion): show how starting with 'Never', 'Rarely', 'Seldom', 'Not only', 'Only after/when', or 'Under no circumstances' triggers question word order (Auxiliary + Subject + Verb).

Quick concept check — whole class

• 'Never I have seen such a busy airport' — how do we fix the word order after 'Never'? ('Never have I seen such a busy airport' — Auxiliary + Subject + Verb.)

• Turn 'Consistency matters most in language learning' into both an 'It-cleft' and a 'What-cleft'. ('It is consistency that matters most…' and 'What matters most in language learning is consistency'.)

• Why is 'It might perhaps possibly rain' weak speaking? (Over-hedging — choose one clear hedge that matches your evidence, such as 'It is likely to rain' or 'It may well rain'.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two contrast tables in Part 3: first, Unhedged Overstatement vs Measured Hedge vs Over-Hedged Doubt; second, Ordinary Word Order vs Cleft Focus and Negative Inversion.

• Drill the inversion rhythm chorally on three sentences: 'Never have I seen…', 'Rarely do we find…', and 'Only after reading the report did I understand…'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 4 minutes to complete Practice A (6 items) individually, checking A1 ('Never'), A2 ('was'), A3 ('did I understand'), and A4 ('suggests / suggest').

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners transform B1 (cleft), B2 (hedge), B3 and B6 (inversion), repair B4 ('Never have I seen…'), and perform B5 in both casual and formal registers.

• Confirm the key whole-class and spotlight why 'Only after reading it twice' in A3 puts the inversion in the main clause ('did I understand').

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. Never · 2. did she pass · 3. did I understand · 4. suggests (or: suggest) · 5. the detailed budget · 6. tend

Practice B: 1. Online learning may well replace some traditional lectures, or tends to complement classroom study. (answers vary) · 2. It was the practical examples that made the lesson easy to follow. · 3. Rarely had we seen such rapid progress in a single term. · 4. Never have I seen such a busy market. · 5. answers vary (e.g. Teammate: 'Could I have two more days on the report?' / Director: 'I was wondering if it might be possible to extend the deadline by two days so we can verify the final figures.') · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Not only does my mentor listen patiently, but she also gives practical advice.')

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'Never' — negative opener triggering 'have I seen'.

• A2 'was' — singular verb after 'What we really need…' ('is' in present, 'was' in past; both 'is' and 'was' can be discussed, with 'was' matching a past context and 'is' present).

• A3 'did I understand' — inversion occurs in the main clause after 'Only after reading it twice…'.

• A4 accepts both 'suggests' (treating 'data' as a singular mass noun) and 'suggest' (treating 'data' as a plural noun in academic style).

• B4 'Never have I seen such a mess' — restores auxiliary-before-subject inversion.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn Panel Discussion model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how the two panellists use 'is likely to', 'It could be argued that', 'It is flexibility that…', 'What organizations need is…', 'tends to', and 'rarely have companies…'.

• Run the four-minute Panel Discussion in pairs on the three future-focused questions in Part 5, requiring each speaker to use at least one hedge, one cleft focus, and one negative inversion across the discussion.

• Have two pairs perform their strongest question-and-challenge exchange for the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: Over the next decade, artificial intelligence is likely to handle most routine scheduling and translation, so it could be argued that memorising facts will matter less than critical thinking. B: I agree, though it is human judgment that clients still trust most in complex decisions. A: Exactly — studies suggest that teams using AI alongside human review tend to make far fewer errors, and rarely have companies succeeded by automating customer relationships completely.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have pairs express one claim at three levels of certainty and complete the three inversion starters ('Never have I…', 'Rarely do we…', 'Only when… did I…') aloud.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise storytelling 'Little did we know that…', diplomatic understatement ('not unreasonable', 'not uncommon'), and formal conditional inversion ('Were we to delay…').

• Have each learner build one 'Little did I know…' sentence about a past surprise.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to choose one topic in Part 7 and jot down keywords for their two-minute persuasive talk: (1) Hedged opening claim + evidence, (2) Cleft focus ('What matters most is…' or 'It is X that…'), and (3) One memorable negative inversion.

• Partners take turns speaking for two full minutes while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it combines 'tends to produce', 'may well save', 'What actually builds fluency is…', 'It is that immediate human response that…', and 'Not only does live conversation train…, but it also…', and have learners polish one sentence of their own.

Student Book model response:

If we want to strengthen education across our country over the next decade, we must look first at practical access. It is reliable internet connectivity in district schools that will determine who benefits from modern learning tools. Rarely have we seen technology advance as rapidly in our major cities as it has in recent years, yet students in smaller towns often study without updated textbooks or digital libraries. Providing solar-powered digital libraries in district centres may well be the most cost-effective educational investment of the decade. Studies suggest that when teachers can share resources easily, classroom engagement rises within a single term. What our students need most is not a more complicated syllabus, but equal access to the tools that already exist.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Evaluate the two-minute talks using the four Partner listening checklist criteria: calibrated hedges (without over-hedging), accurate cleft focus, one well-formed negative inversion, and measured, persuasive delivery.

• Remind learners that inversion is like spice: one negative inversion in a two-minute talk is memorable; five in a row sounds unnatural.

• Collect two anonymous inversion or cleft slips for the closing board repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two oral recall tasks in Part 8 (stating one claim at three certainty levels and producing one 'It-cleft', one 'What-cleft', and one 'Never/Rarely' inversion from memory).

• Have learners tick the self-check boxes and review Formula Book Card 15 if needed.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Keep the three-tool board chart visible during Parts 5 and 7 so developing speakers can pick one hedge, one cleft, and one inversion frame with confidence.

• Write three ready-to-use inversion starters with the auxiliary already attached: 'Never have I…' · 'Rarely do we…' · 'Not only did…, but…'

• If a learner forgets to invert after 'Not only' or 'Rarely', point to the Direct Question rule: 'Put have/do/did before the subject, just like a question.'

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Encourage confident speakers to use 'Only after/when + clause + did/have + subject + verb' and one diplomatic litotes phrase ('not unreasonable') during Part 7.

• Challenge stronger panellists in Part 5 to ask a tough follow-up question ('What evidence do you have for that?') so their partner has to calibrate their certainty live.

• Ask early finishers to compare the emphasis of 'We need time' vs 'What we need is time' vs 'It is time that we need'.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• 'Rarely we see such commitment.' → 'Rarely do we see such commitment.' — Fix: insert 'do/does/did' when inverting a simple verb without an existing auxiliary.

• 'Only after the meeting ended I realised the mistake.' → 'Only after the meeting ended did I realise the mistake.' — Fix: invert the main clause ('did I realise'), not the 'after' clause.

• 'It might maybe possibly work.' → 'It may well work / It could work.' — Fix: use one clear hedge.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two panel questions in Part 5.

• Do the certainty scale and three core inversions in Part 6 in class and assign 'Little did I know…' as homework.

• Run a 90-second Real Talk speech per partner and close with the Part 8 oral recall check.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Exit ticket: each learner says one 'What… is…' cleft sentence and one 'Never/Rarely' inversion before leaving.

• Remind learners that clefts, hedging, and inversion are tested in the Final Assessment (A12, B6, B8, C3) and are key markers of top rubric performance in Lesson 16.

• Point learners to Formula Book Card 15 in Appendix 1 for revision.

• Feedback focus: Highlight one well-calibrated hedge and one natural cleft or inversion you heard during Part 7. Then put two anonymous inversion word-order slips on the board for a 60-second class repair.

LESSON 16 · GRAMMAR IN REAL CONVERSATION — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: bring all the course grammar together in free, accurate, confident speech

This guide follows the exact eight-part sequence of the Student Book lesson. Teach the whole class together through the shared explanations and activities, using the support and extension notes below to help every speaker succeed.

Lesson outcomes, preparation, and 60-minute timing

Lesson objectives:

• Integrate the entire sixteen-lesson course by selecting structures across the Four Jobs of Grammar in Spoken English: TIME, CHOICE, SHAPE, and STYLE.

• Use natural self-repair phrases ('What I mean is…', 'Let me rephrase that — …', 'Or rather, …') to fix slips in real time without freezing or losing conversational flow.

• Deliver an unscripted two-minute culminating speech under Final Assessment conditions, combining at least six distinct grammar structures and handling live follow-up questions.

Observable success criteria — listen for learners who:

✓ learners identify and explain the grammatical reason behind all six cross-course repairs in Practice A

✓ in the four-round Grammar Gym (Part 5) and culminating Real Talk speech (Part 7), speakers combine structures across all four grammar jobs (TIME, CHOICE, SHAPE, STYLE)

✓ when a slip occurs in speech, learners use a natural repair phrase and keep talking smoothly

Before class begins:

• Draw the Four-Job Map across the board: 1. TIME (Tenses · Narrative tenses · Reported speech) · 2. CHOICE (Modals · Conditionals · Wishes/preferences) · 3. SHAPE (Questions · Linkers · Passives · Causatives · Gerunds/infinitives · Relatives · Participles) · 4. STYLE (Comparisons · Hedging · Clefts · Inversion).

• Write the three live self-repair phrases on the board: 'What I mean is…' · 'Let me rephrase that — …' · 'Or rather, …'.
