Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Have pairs read the two responses in Part 1 aloud (Speaker A's safe, repetitive past-simple sentences vs Speaker B's rich, multi-structure reflection) and identify the grammar tools Speaker B combined.

• Run the 45-second hook warm-up: Partner A speaks on 'A skill I am proud of learning' while Partner B listens and names at least three grammar structures from the course that they heard.

• Celebrate how far the class has come: today is about bringing every tool together in real conversation and learning how to self-repair like a confident speaker.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 (The Four Jobs of Grammar in Spoken English): have learners locate each of the fifteen previous lessons on the Four-Job Map so they see the entire course as one connected toolkit.

• Teach Rule 2 (The 3-step speaking habit: Think of the message → Choose the frame → Say the chunk whole) and Rule 3 (Self-repair in live conversation): model making a deliberate tense slip and repairing it smoothly with 'or rather…' without apologising or stopping.

Quick concept check — whole class

• Name the Four Jobs of Grammar in Spoken English and one structure that belongs to each job. (TIME: tenses/reported speech; CHOICE: modals/conditionals/wishes; SHAPE: questions/linkers/passives/causatives/gerunds/relatives/participles; STYLE: comparisons/hedging/clefts/inversion.)

• If you hear yourself say 'I live here since 2021' in the middle of an interview, what is the smooth way to repair it without stopping? ('I live here — or rather, I've lived here since 2021…')

• Why is 'One clear complex structure per sentence' better advice than stacking five advanced structures into a single sentence? (Because clarity and natural communication always come first.)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Walk through the two tables in Part 3: first, Safe Flat Speech vs Integrated Confident Speech across Storytelling, Advice, and Argument; second, Freezing on a Mistake vs Natural Self-Repair.

• Have pairs practise the three self-repair lines in Table 2 aloud so the rhythm of 'or rather…' and 'what I mean is…' feels completely natural.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Give learners 5 minutes to complete Practice A (6 cross-course error repairs) in pairs: insist that for every item, learners state both the corrected sentence and the lesson rule behind it.

• Run Practice B (6 items) in pairs: learners combine B1 (participle), report B2, compare with 'far' in B3, invert B4 ('Never have I…'), hedge B5, and ask the polite indirect question in B6.

• Confirm the key whole-class — these 12 items serve as a rapid warm-up across the whole syllabus.

Answer key and teaching notes (Practice A & B)

Practice A: 1. I finished my university degree in 2022. ('in 2022' is a finished past time → past simple) · 2. If the flight is delayed tomorrow, we will call the hotel. (ordinary future condition → present simple after 'if') · 3. Despite the cold wind, we walked to the summit. / Although the wind was cold, we walked to the summit. · 4. My supervisor suggested attending the workshop. / …suggested that I attend the workshop. ('suggest' takes -ing or a that-clause, never 'me to') · 5. Never have I felt so proud of our team. (negative opener triggers auxiliary + subject inversion) · 6. We really look forward to hosting your delegation next month. ('to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition → verb-ing)

Practice B: 1. Not having slept the night before, he made several small calculation errors. · 2. She told me not to worry about the deadline. / She reassured me that I didn't need to worry about the deadline. · 3. answers vary (e.g. 'Practising out loud is far more effective than silent reading because it trains your mouth and ear to work together in real time.') · 4. Tomorrow's examination schedule has been changed (by the committee). · 5. This new teaching method may well be one of the most effective for many learners. / This new teaching method tends to work very well for most learners. (answers vary) · 6. Could you tell me what time tomorrow's rehearsal starts? / Do you know what time tomorrow's rehearsal starts?

Explanatory notes and common traps:

• A1 'I saw that film last night' — finished past time ('last night') requires past simple (Lesson 1).

• A2 'Could you tell me where the station is?' — indirect question takes statement word order (Lesson 3).

• A3 'If I had known earlier, I would have helped you' — third conditional uses 'if + past perfect' (Lesson 5).

• A4 'Despite the rain, the match continued' — 'despite' never takes 'of' (Lesson 8).

• A5 'I look forward to hearing from you' — preposition 'to' takes '-ing' (Lesson 11).

• A6 'My brother, who lives in Herat, is an architect' — non-defining clause after a comma takes 'who', never 'that' (Lesson 12).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Read the 3-turn Grammar Gym model exchange in Part 5 aloud so learners hear how two partners move from narrative tenses and reported advice to third conditionals, comparisons, linkers, and relative clauses.

• Run the four-round 'Grammar Gym' in pairs (1 minute per round: Round 1 Storytelling, Round 2 Advice & Hypotheticals, Round 3 Briefing & Description, Round 4 Persuasion & Style) while the listener counts how many target structures land naturally in each round.

• Ask two pairs to replay their strongest 60-second round for the class.

Sample partner exchange for classroom demonstration

A: Two years ago I almost gave up speaking English in meetings because I was afraid of making grammar slips. B: What changed your mind? A: My mentor told me to focus on delivering the message first and suggested recording myself for two minutes a day. If I hadn't followed her advice, I wouldn't feel nearly as confident as I do today. B: So what would you recommend for our school? A: What we need is a weekly speaking club where learners can practise real conversations without fear.

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

• Run the first block of Part 6 ('Make the core pattern automatic'): have each learner pick the one lesson from earlier in the course that they found most challenging, turn to its Formula Book card in Appendix 1, and produce three true spoken sentences using that pattern.

• Move to the second block ('Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus'): practise combining two structures in a single sentence ('Had I known how useful speaking clubs were, I would have joined one in my first semester, which would have saved me months of hesitation') and opening a talk with a 'What-cleft' or 'Given…' frame.

• Have pairs do a 30-second deliberate self-repair drill: Partner A starts a sentence with a deliberate slip and repairs it smoothly mid-sentence using 'What I mean is…' or 'Or rather…'.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give learners 30 seconds to plan their culminating two-minute talk using the three-part plan in Part 7 (1. A past story or turning point; 2. How that experience shapes their work/studies today; 3. One change or recommendation they would make for future learners) and choose one structure from each of the Four Jobs.

• Partners take turns speaking for two full minutes without reading, then answer two unscripted follow-up questions from their partner while the listener checks the four Partner listening checklist criteria.

• Uncover the Model response, trace how it integrates narrative tenses, reported advice, a third conditional, present perfect, a concession linker, a cleft sentence, a modified comparison, a live self-repair ('or rather, have been practising'), and a closing inversion ('Rarely have I felt…'), and have learners celebrate their progress.

Student Book model response:

Two years ago, I used to avoid speaking English in group meetings because I was afraid of making mistakes — while others were sharing their ideas, I would translate every sentence in my head until the moment had passed. Joining a weekly speaking circle, which a colleague recommended to me, was the turning point that changed that habit. Within a month, I had met partners who corrected me encouragingly, and I realised that communication is about clarity, not perfection. Since then, I've been practising aloud almost every day, and my supervisor has noticed the difference. Next spring I'm going to take the TOEFL exam so that I can apply for a graduate programme. If I keep building one small habit at a time, the score will take care of itself. What matters most to me now is staying calm under pressure — and that comes only from using my voice every day.

How to guide and assess this task:

• Use this culminating two-minute talk and follow-up exchange as a full dress rehearsal for the Final Assessment speaking task (using the 16-point Evaluation Rubric in the Final Assessment).

• Treat every smooth self-repair ('or rather…', 'what I mean is…') as positive evidence of grammatical control and communicative confidence.

• Compare learners' confidence, range, and fluency today with their baseline diagnostic speaking sample from the start of the course.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• With books closed, have pairs complete the two final oral recall tasks in Part 8 (naming the Four Jobs of Grammar with one example each, and delivering a 60-second reflection on how their spoken English has changed during the course).

• Have learners complete the self-check boxes and turn to Appendix 4 (Can-Do Tracker) to tick their 'After Lesson 16' column across all sixteen lessons.

Supporting and stretching one mixed classroom

Supporting developing speakers within the shared task:

• Leave the Four-Job Map and the three Self-Repair Phrases visible on the board throughout Parts 5 and 7 so every speaker has a clear visual roadmap.

• Remind developing speakers that three or four accurate, well-linked structures in a two-minute talk sound far stronger than rushed, over-complicated sentences.

• If a speaker freezes mid-sentence, prompt gently with 'What I mean is…' so they experience recovering and finishing their thought.

Stretching confident speakers toward deeper precision:

• Challenge confident speakers to include at least one structure from each of the Four Jobs plus one deliberate cleft or negative inversion in their two-minute speech.

• Encourage stronger listeners during the Part 7 follow-up exchange to ask one hypothetical question ('What would have happened if…?') and one evaluative question ('Why do you think that matters most?').

• Have early finishers compare their 'Before course' and 'After Lesson 16' columns in Appendix 4 and set three concrete speaking goals for the next month.

Common misunderstandings, 45-minute plan, and feedback

High-frequency slips and rapid board repairs:

• Freezing or apologising after a grammar slip ('Sorry, my English is bad…') → Fix: replace apologies with a calm repair phrase ('Or rather, …') and keep going.

• Over-loading a single sentence with too many clauses → Fix: end the sentence cleanly and start the next sentence with a clear linker or focus frame.

• Dropping back into only present simple and past simple under time pressure → Fix: jot down two specific target frames ('Having…', 'What matters most is…') during the 30-second planning window.

Adapting for a 45-minute session:

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 minutes; run two rounds of the Grammar Gym in Part 5 (Storytelling + Persuasion).

• Do the self-repair drill in Part 6 in class and assign the Appendix 4 Can-Do Tracker reflection as preparation for the Final Assessment.

• Keep the full two-minute Real Talk speech in Part 7 — it is the culminating speaking milestone of the course.

Closing recall and fluency-protecting feedback:

• Celebrate completion of all sixteen lessons! Have each learner share one structure from the course that now feels part of their natural voice.

• The next session is the Final Assessment (Part 1: 30-item grammar assessment; Part 2: two-minute independent speaking task + follow-up exchange).

• Encourage learners to review Formula Book Cards 1–16 (Appendix 1) and the Common Errors Guide (Appendix 2) before the Final Assessment.

• Feedback focus: Make your final lesson feedback celebratory and specific: name one concrete strength you heard from the class in each of the Four Jobs (Time, Choice, Shape, Style) and praise every speaker who used a live self-repair phrase to keep their conversation flowing.

ASSESSMENT GUIDANCE

Keys, acceptable alternatives, and scoring spoken progress

How the assessments work together

• Lesson Practice A and B keys: printed inside every lesson guide (and in Student Book Appendix 5).

• Diagnostic Test, Review Tests 1–3, and Final Assessment keys: printed below for instructor reference.

• Open-ended speaking tasks: evaluate using the lesson's observable criteria and the four-criterion speaking rubric (Grammatical accuracy · Appropriate structure selection · Clarity · Successful communication; 1–4 points each, total 16).

Fair marking principles

• Credit every grammatical alternative listed in the key (and any other natural form that accurately fulfils the prompt and context).

• For sentence transformations and open prompts, judge whether the target structure and meaning are accurate rather than requiring identical wording.

• Do not compare the 25-item Diagnostic raw score with the 30-item Final Assessment raw score as a numerical gain claim — the two written tests have different lengths and blueprints. Instead, compare learners' baseline and final speaking scores across the four rubric criteria under identical task conditions.

Model final speaking response (one strong example, not a script)

Approximately two minutes, delivered without reading

A decision that changed my life was moving to Kabul for university.
At first I had never lived away from my family, and I was not sure I could manage alone. While I was adjusting, I made mistakes — I spent too much on transport because I had not learned the bus routes. If I had known the city better, I would have saved both time and money, and I would be more relaxed now. I believe education is an investment, although it was hard to leave home. I was told that grades would depend on attendance, so I attended every class. I have enjoyed meeting people who come from other provinces; the diversity has taught me patience. I have decided to continue studying even though costs are high. What I hope to do next is pass the TOEFL and teach English — the course has shown me that speaking every day is the key. Never have I been more certain that effort, not talent, decides who improves.

Use this sample to calibrate rubric scoring with colleagues: identify how the speaker combines narrative tenses, conditionals, passives, relative clauses, hedging, and cleft focus, and remember that any student response that meets the four criteria in the student's own voice deserves full marks.

Keys — Diagnostic Test and Review Tests

Diagnostic

A. 1. saw · 2. has worked / has been working · 3. was cooking · 4. had worked / had been working; 'worked' is also possible with before · 5. boils · 6. were building · 7. have lost · 8. went · 9. have read · 10. had already left

B. 1. rains · 2. knew · 3. repairing / to be repaired · 4. was written · 5. leaving · 6. the station is · 7. who / that · 8. didn't smoke · 9. more intelligent · 10. did she finish

C. 1. can't · 2. Despite · 3. where I lived / where I live (if still true) · 4. may / might / could · 5. had / got

Review Test 1

A. 1. haven't seen · 2. were waiting · 3. freezes · 4. is studying · 5. had eaten · 6. is going to rain / will rain · 7. have / known · 8. started

B. 1. must · 2. Would / closing · 3. is · 4. don't have to / needn't

C. 1. Answers vary; e.g., 'You should rest before driving.' (should + base verb) · 2. Could you tell me where you parked? · 3. must be

Review Test 2

A. 1. knew · 2. had taken · 3. more effective · 4. was reading · 5. had already left · 6. made · 7. best · 8. hurry

B. 1. Despite the exam being hard, everyone passed. / Despite the difficulty, everyone passed. · 2. If I had a car, I would drive you. / If I had a car, I could drive you. · 3. answers vary — advice with should/could/might · 4. Could you tell me where the bank is?

C. 1. If she had saved money, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy… · 2. answers vary — far + comparative + reason · 3. Despite the cost, we decided to proceed.

Review Test 3

A. 1. was built · 2. repaired · 3. to speak · 4. making · 5. where · 6. whose · 7. didn't mention · 8. knew

B. 1. The room needs cleaning. / The room needs to be cleaned. · 2. He must have missed the train. · 3. Students interested in the course should apply. · 4. It is believed that the economy is improving. / The economy is believed to be improving.

C. 1. more / more confident · 2. Do you know where the bank is? · 3. had · 4. I enjoy reading novels.

Key — Final Assessment (30 items)

A. 1. have lived / 've lived / have been living · 2. had already had · 3. is · 4. hadn't said · 5. was cancelled · 6. must have been working · 7. making · 8. rewrite · 9. challenging · 10. Warned / Having been warned · 11. leaving · 12. did she apologise

B. 1. He said he would help me the next day. · 2. She asked me where I had bought it. · 3. Could you tell me when the shop closes? · 4. If he had revised, he wouldn't have failed. · 5. The documents have been stolen. · 6. It was the manager who/that approved the plan. · 7. I had the roof fixed. · 8. Rarely had she felt so confident. · 9. Although the task was difficult, they finished it. · 10. Having studied hard, he passed easily.

C. 1. can't · 2. Despite · 3. This method may well be the best. / This method is probably the best. (answers vary) · 4. Option A is far better than Option B because… (answers vary) · 5. The book (that / which) I read was amazing. · 6. more confident · 7. She advised me to apply early. · 8. meeting

Explanatory notes on key test items

• Review Test 1 A4 ('is studying'): 'these days' frames an ongoing current project; past simple would clash with the time cue.

• Review Test 1 B1 ('must') vs B4 ('don't have to / needn't'): B1 expresses a legal requirement, whereas B4 expresses absence of obligation (not 'mustn't', which means forbidden).

• Review Test 2 B1: credit both 'Despite the exam being hard, everyone passed' and 'Despite the difficulty, everyone passed' — both avoid attaching 'being hard' to 'everyone'.

• Review Test 3 A3 ('to speak'): passive reporting structure from Lesson 9 ('She is said to speak five languages').

• Final Assessment A1: credit 'have lived', ''ve lived', and 'have been living' — all three accurately express a situation continuing up to now with 'since 2020'.

• Final Assessment C3 & C4: credit any well-formed hedge ('may well', 'probably', 'tends to', 'is likely to') on C3 and any accurate degree modifier + comparative + reason on C4.

• Diagnostic Test: credit all listed alternatives ('has worked / has been working', 'who / that', 'may / might / could', 'had / got').
